maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF NATO SECRETARY GENERAL

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF NATO SECRETARY GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have with us in the gallery today the secretary general of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, Mr. Dirk Stikker, who is making his first official visit to Canada since taking over his present responsibilities in April. This is not the first time he has been in Canada. His first visit goes back to 1946, and in the intervening years he has been here on more than one occasion. As the house knows, Mr. Stikker has a long and distinguished record in the field of foreign affairs. He was foreign minister of the Netherlands from 1948 to 1952. My colleagues and I greatly appreciate the opportunity he has given us of discussing with him not only the problems of NATO but generally of the international situation today.
I feel that I speak for all hon. members in welcoming Mr. Stikker and in expressing to him the hope that under his direction the alliance will continue to develop its strength and unity, and that the greatest possible use will continue to be made of the NATO council for intensive consultations on the critical issues currently facing the NATO partners. On behalf of the house I extend to him a warm welcome.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF NATO SECRETARY GENERAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I on behalf of the opposition join very warmly in the welcome the Prime Minister has extended to the new secretary general of NATO, who is paying his first visit to Ottawa in this capacity. I do so officially, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of a party which has supported and will continue to support a strong and united NATO as a bulwark of defence and peace. Perhaps I might be permitted to say that I also do so personally as an old friend and colleague of Mr. Stikker.

maintopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF NATO SECRETARY GENERAL
speechtext:

subtopic: STATEMENT ON FALL-OUT RESULTING FROM RECENT TESTS

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monleilh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: STATEMENT ON FALL-OUT RESULTING FROM RECENT TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a statement on fall-out resulting from the resumption of nuclear tests by the Soviet union. Since the first test explosion on September 1, my department's network of 24 air sampling stations located across Canada has continued to provide regular material for analysis on a daily basis. From the results obtained, it now appears that effects of the Russian testing program have been observed at some of our stations.
For example, on September 7, the reading for Edmonton showed a fresh fall-out level of nine disintegrations per minute per cubic metre of air, a value which was about 30 times higher than the levels observed for this station during the past several months. This is the most significant increase recorded for samples received to date, although a value of four units, or 15 times higher than normal, was observed for Winnipeg on September 8, and a value of one unit or three times higher than normal for Calgary on September 7.
As I have previously indicated to the house, the significance of all radioactivity data from the health viewpoint can only be assessed on the basis of average levels for a reasonable period of time, perhaps up to a year. The observations we have made in the air monitoring program have consistently shown large fluctuations from day to day, and it is interesting to note that the level observed for Calgary on September 8, the day after the high reading, was back to normal.

Nuclear Fall-out Results In attempting to interpret the present situation I think it is appropriate to refer to the recommendations of the international commission on radiological protection, which provide the basic data for calculating the maximum permissible level for the public at large. From these data, a level of 6.6 units has been derived. In this connection it is important to realize that the calculations imply continued exposure at this level throughout a lifetime. Short duration increases above this limit are not considered to be of serious public health concern.
Furthermore, it is of interest to note that measurements of fall-out levels in air were made during and subsequent to the extensive weapons testing programs of the fall of 1958. These data were collected by the national research council as part of Canada's contribution to the international geophysical year project. Nine of the observing stations were located in areas now served by our present program, and for these stations the highest over-all monthly average reached a value of 6.88 units in February, 1959. During the same period, however, individual daily results were as high as 38.1 units. Six months later, when my department's program began operating, the monthly average had dropped to 0.85 units and it has subsequently continued to decrease to the point where the over-all monthly average for July, 1961, was 0.29.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON FALL-OUT RESULTING FROM RECENT TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will want to examine carefully the announcement on radioactive levels given this morning by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It is evident from the statement of the minister that his announcement is of great significance. An indication of an increase in levels following recent test explosions is something that cannot be ignored in this or any other country.
We are fortunate in Canada in having a testing system, which I believe we owe largely to the late Dr. Cipriani and Dr. Watkinson, one that can take its place with any similar system in any country of the world.
The minister did not tell us whether the increased radiation was of a character which would warrant our concluding that there was a substantial increase in the danger to human health. We do know that the best scientific opinion as of 1956 suggested that for the population at large the concentration of radioactive strontium should not exceed one tenth of that permitted to the small number of persons employed in radioactive industries. But we have not been told by the minister whether the dangers from these levels are to be compared with the dangers that flow from traditional uses of materials from which have emanated dangerous radio-


activity over the years. In any event, the minister's statement is a forceful demonstration of the undesirability of nuclear testing at this time.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON FALL-OUT RESULTING FROM RECENT TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare is a further confirmation of the opinion of mankind generally that the resumption of nuclear explosions was a mistake and is against the best interests of the people of the world no matter in which country they reside. The evidence presented this morning is a clear indication of the dangers that flow from a continuation of such weapons testing, and would indicate that once again in Canada there may be evidence, as was the case a few years ago, of some contamination of food.
This demonstrates once again the need for Canada and other nations to pursue a policy of support for an international agreement that would prohibit the testing of nuclear weapons. We think this is an indication that those members both in the government party and in the opposition who are so strongly in favour of the abolition of weapons testing should redouble their efforts.

These target area headquarters will be put into operation in the coming months. They are located near principal cities. These sites will be manned by military personnel, who will work closely with both municipal and provincial authorities in controlling search, rescue and re-entry operations in areas that may be attacked. In most cases the new target area headquarters will be located some 20 to 50 miles from the major cities.
Thirteen of the projected 16 sites have been selected. They are as follows: Windsor for Halifax, N.S.; Camp Gagetown for Saint John, N.B.; Camp Valcartier for Quebec City, Que.; St. Jerome for Montreal, Qpe.; Almonte for Ottawa, Ont.; Newmarket for Toronto, Ont.; Chatham for Windsor, Ont.; Dunnville for Niagara Falls, Ont.; Portage La Prairie for Winnipeg, Man.; Wetaskiwin for Edmonton, Alta.; Olds for Calgary, Alta.; Camp Chilliwack for Vancouver, B.C.; and Duncan for Victoria, B.C.
Other sites for the cities of St. John's, Newfoundland, Hamilton and London, Ont., have not yet been decided. They will be announced in the near future.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the first opportunity I have had of presenting the estimates of the Department of National Defence to the committee. I appreciate the privilege. It gives me a very welcome opportunity to speak on the important subject of our military security. But before I do so I should like to say a word about my very distinguished predecessor in office, General George Pearkes, V.C., now His Honour the Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia.
I have had the privilege of a long acquaintanceship and close friendship with George Pearkes, extending back to the early 1920's. I served in the first Canadian division under his command, and we entered parliament at the same time. He is a distinguished soldier who rendered signal service to Canada during the first war, between the wars, and throughout the second world war. His interest in and concern for the defence of Canada was demonstrated throughout his years in parliament and particularly as minister of national defence for nearly three and a half years. He is a great gentleman and a great Canadian, and I am sure we all wish him well in his present distinguished position.
I do not think anyone would deny that we are living in times of great stress. Important and far reaching changes are taking place hi many parts of the world; new nations are emerging, resulting on occasion in violence and bloodshed. But overriding all other considerations is the open threat of the Soviet union to eventually achieve world domination. This threat is being implemented on many fronts, economic, political, ideological and military. To combat it requires counteraction in all these areas.
Today, however, I intend to deal with the military threat to our national security. That it continues to exist was made very clear by the Soviet premier earlier this year, when he warned of the consequences which would follow if nations tried to resist the communist move to world wide acceptance of this
Supply-National Defence organization of society. I might add that Mr. Khrushchev went on to say that one of the means for preventing a new war is the development of peace fronts throughout the world, including pacifists of all political beliefs, and through a policy of peaceful coexistence-as defined by him, of course, meaning acceptance of communism. This policy, he said:
facilitates the activities of the communist party and other progressive organizations of the working class in the capitalist countries, makes it easier for the peoples to combat aggressive war blocs and foreign military bases and contributes to the success of the national liberation government. The policy of peaceful coexistence is, thus, so far as its social content is concerned, a form of intense economic, political and ideological struggle between the proletariat and the aggressive forces of imperialism in the world arena.
I think that reinforces what the Leader of the Opposition said a day or two ago to the effect that words have been debased, and they no longer mean, in the Soviet lexicon, what they mean in ours.
In recent weeks, of course, we have been confronted with a series of threats with regard to the Berlin situation. I shall be referring later to the steps the government has taken in the light of the present international situation.
The government's defence policy has two objectives; first, to maintain peace by preventing a third global war; and second, to prevent subjection to a foreign power. Everything we do in defence is devoted to attaining these two purposes.
We believe they can best be attained by a system of alliances, and thus we have been strong supporters of, and have been taking and will continue to take our full part in, making NATO, NORAD and the UN effective. History has shown that had the coalitions that won the last two world wars been in existence and firmly united before the wars, those wars might well have been avoided. When in 1948 it became apparent that the west was again faced with a situation where one by one the countries of Europe might fall under communist domination, the formation of the North Atlantic treaty coalition was the logical step to take. Canada pressed for this action and has firmly supported it since then. It is the cornerstone of our defence policy.
Working as a member of a group of nations is an art that is not easily acquired. To play an effective part, individual nations must show that they are prepared to accept their responsibilities and to make sacrifices, sacrifices in money, men or risks. Only so long as the will of the individual members remains steadfast will the coaltion be strong and its will to stand together be abundantly clear to any would-be aggressor. Canada must, therefore,

Supply-National Defence maintain her proper share of forces committed to NATO, and show to her fellow members and to any possible opponent a determination to stand with the coalition against any aggression.
If membership in NATO demands some abrogation of national freedom of action, it has advantages that far outweigh any drawbacks. The strength of the union is the sum of the strengths of the individual members, and the total strength of the west thus marshalled is formidable indeed. Individual members do not have to maintain a balance of all the forces that go to make up modern military power. Individual members can contribute to the whole those forces that best suit their national circumstances. Canada, for example, does not attempt to provide strategic bombers, intercontinental ballistic missiles or fast carrier task forces; yet the NATO organization has the necessary forces in these categories.
I think one of the difficulties which many people experience in their thinking on defence is that they tend to think of Canada particularly as a nation which in their view should be in a position to maintain a force of all kinds, which at the present time is a complete impossibility.
A very important part of the NATO philosophy is the reliance on the retaliatory nuclear forces maintained by the United States and the United Kingdom. Canada does not contribute directly to these forces, but she does make an important contribution to ensure that the major portion of these forces remains effective. By this I mean that through the maintenance, together with the United States, of the early warning radar lines and the anti-bomber defences, she is ensuring that retaliation would be of such an order as to cause equal, if not greater, destruction on the territory of those responsible for launching an attack on this continent.
In North America, a regional area of NATO, the defence against air attack is a single problem. It cannot be separated into parts by boundary lines or limits of territorial waters. This fact was recognized during world war II, when joint plans for defence were drawn up and co-ordinated between the United States and ourselves. After the war, when it became apparent that there was an increasing risk from the air, further closer collaboration in planning took place. Eventually, because of the increasing speeds of aircraft and the resulting shorter and shorter reaction time, consultation and co-ordination were too time consuming, and it was decided to form a joint headquarters to control the air defence forces of the two partner nations
[Mr. Harkness.l
so as to make the most effective use of the very short warning time available to the defences.
NORAD has been attacked as an organization wherein Canada might lose some element of sovereignty. Theoretically I suppose any international agreement involves some loss of sovereignty, but I do not consider that there is any significant loss of Canadian sovereignty involved in the NORAD agreement. The Canadian forces remain under Canadian command. Only operational control is exercised by the joint headquarters of NORAD, and there is no intrusion of United States forces or United States authority in areas that were not already provided for under the former co-ordinated arrangements.
I would like to stress again that the NORAD agreement is a purely defensive agreement. Military action can only be taken if North America comes under attack from the air. In other words, it cannot by any conceivable circumstance start a war. The commander in chief of NORAD is responsible to the Canadian and the United States governments through their respective chiefs of staff, and these governments can and do exercise control over the planning and operating procedures and actions that NORAD takes.
Our contribution to the United Nations is,
I think, well known. We have substantial forces in Egypt, and our servicemen take part in a number of truce commissions and supervisory bodies in various trouble spots in the world. In the last year, of course, we have taken on the additional responsibility of providing some 300 army and air force personnel to the United Nations force in the Congo.
I have just given a broad outline of our general defence policy. Before going on to some more specific matters I should like to briefly mention some opposing ideas which have been put forward from various quarters.
As an alternative to the collective security arrangements we have entered into, other proposals have been put forth, in many cases after genuine and sincere consideration, generally motivated, I think, by the very real fear of nuclear attack on Canada. Some have suggested unilateral disarmament. Presumably the thinking is that if Canada were completely disarmed there would be no provocation for attack. This theory, of course, ignores history; it ignores our geographical position, and it ignores the stated policy of the Soviet. I submit that it is completely unacceptable to Canadians as a whole. It would neither ensure our security nor enhance our reputation in the eyes of the world. To suggest that such an action would have a profound effect on Russia, China or any

other communist regime displays a naivete that is beyond reasonable comprehension.
In talking or writing about defence policy, many people have become so obsessed with equipment matters-in other words the kind of aircraft and armaments available-that they have come to look upon these as the main features of defence policy rather than as one of the means by which basic defence policy is carried into effect. The type of equipment secured depends on the strategy being followed to implement our defence policy and on the tactics which it is believed we will have to employ. Essentially this means that our forces must be equipped to give them the maximum possible mobility and flexibility. It requires that they be equipped with weapons comparable to if not better than those of a potential adversary. It is the policy of the government that our forces should not be required to face a potential enemy with inferior weapons.
Inevitably there will continue to be much argument about the various items of equipment supplied to the services, or which various people think should be supplied to them. Contrary to the statements which have frequently been made that the services, particularly the army, have chiefly old and obsolete equipment, they have in fact been supplied with an almost completely new range of equipment of all kinds.
Three weapons systems-the Honest John surface to surface missile, the Bomarc antiaircraft weapon and the CF-104 aircraftbeing obtained have a nuclear capability, but I should like to make it clear that their military role can in no way be compared with such strategic nuclear weapons as are maintained by the United Kingdom, the United States and the Soviet union. Defensive weapons with a nuclear capability may be required to maintain the credibility of the deterrent, and in the event that the worst happened would be required to provide an effective defence against Soviet aggression. A considerable lead time is necessary for the provision of any such weapons, amounting in most cases to two or three years or more, and it is only prudent to obtain the weapons systems now so that they will be available and our forces trained to use them. The situation is much the same as that of a man living in a lonely cabin in the woods who fears he may be attacked by a bear. He does not wait until the bear actually attacks him to buy a rifle, but secures it beforehand and has it ready in the event of need.
The Bomarc will form part of the defences we must maintain against the manned bomber as long as there are potentially hostile aircraft in existence that could be used against us. A bomber, if unopposed, is by far the
Supply-National Defence best and most effective way of delivering atomic weapons, and it is necessary therefore that we maintain a defence against such a threat as long as it is in existence. We do not know how many long range missiles of adequate accuracy the Russians possess, but we do know that the number is limited. On the other hand, it is a fact that they do have a considerable number of manned aircraft in operation, and should an attack be decided upon it must be presumed that these aircraft would be used.
That was the reason for the decision to improve our air defence by the acquisition of the Bomarc surface to air missile, new heavy radars and the SAGE control system. That was also the reason for the agreement concluded with the United States calling for the acquisition by the R.C.A.F. of 66 F-101B interceptor aircraft. The F-101B is considered the best two place interceptor for service in NORAD today. Five squadrons of 12 aircraft will be formed, one each at Comox,
B.C., North Bay and Ottawa, Ontario, Bagot-ville, Quebec, and Chatham, N.B. Squadrons will be converted progressively with CF-lOO's being withdrawn as each squadron commences conversion.
As part of the agreement the R.C.A.F. will take over the operation and maintenance costs of 11 Pine Tree radars now operated by the United States air force and the maintenance costs of a further five radars now manned by the R.C.A.F. but financed by the United States. The take-over of the 11 radars will be carried out progressively, and present plans are that the program will be completed within a two year period. Canada also assumes financial responsibility for the five radars now manned by the R.C.A.F. as from the date of the agreement.
One other aspect of the agreement relates to the production of the F-104 aircraft by Canadair for our allies. This is a matter not strictly within the purview of the Department of National Defence but it does emphasize, I think, the important part this aircraft has in the over-all equipment policy being implemented by several member nations of NATO.
Other aircraft recently being taken into service or in production will materially strengthen the capabilities of the R.C.A.F. New transport aircraft, including the long range CC-106-the Yukon-the C-130B and the medium range CC-109 will not only increase the over-all air transport capacity of the R.C.A.F., but will also greatly facilitate the movement of Canadian army personnel and equipment to whatever part of the world a requirement exists for our forces.
Canadian production of the CF-104, the aircraft selected to replace the Sabres now being

Supply-National Defence flown in the No. 1 air division, is proceeding according to plan, and this aircraft will enter operational service in 1962. As was announced in 1959, it was selected to meet a specific NATO requirement. It is interesting to note that since then several NATO countries, including Germany, Belgium and The Netherlands, have announced their intention to procure F-104 aircraft. These three countries will all use the F-104 in three roles; as a fighter bomber, an all-weather interceptor and for tactical reconnaissance. It is also expected that Italy will obtain a number of F-104 aircraft, and apart from the NATO countries Japan intends to equip its self defence air force with the F-104. In fact, the F-104 has turned out to be the nearest approach to standardization of aircraft within NATO which has been achieved to date.
For a number of years now the Royal Canadian Navy has been developing methods to combat the submarine menace which exists off both our western and eastern shores. This threat has been further aggravated by the development of the missile capable of being launched from both the surface of the water and under the surface. Continuous improvements have been made to our naval vessels, one notable achievement being the variable depth sonar, product of our own Canadian research teams. This year authority has been given for the installation of helicopter platforms on a number of our destroyer escorts, and additional helicopters will be obtained for anti-submarine duties from these ships. In May last the navy took delivery of the submarine H.M.C.S. Grilse which has been lent by the United States navy. The procurement of this submarine, manned by Canadian naval personnel, will enable our anti-submarine forces on the west coast to get valuable and essential training in the months and years ahead. Ships and aircraft on our east coast for a number of years have had the same facilities provided by submarines of the United Kingdom navy.
The three army brigade groups in Canada, together with members of the reserve forces, have in the past year, in addition to their normal field exercises, been undergoing intensive training in survival operations. New survival equipment has been issued, and the recent exercise Tocsin '61 proved that while a lot remains to be done, great advances have been made in a short space of time in this important aspect of national survival.
The operations of the defence research board are, I think, well known to members of the committee, and I do not intend at this time to outline in detail its various activities. However, I should like to say that within the concept of collective security the board is an essential component of our defence structure.
[Mr. Harkness.l
COMMONS	.
The importance of the place which defence science holds in present day and future planning cannot be too strongly emphasized. Without the advice of a competent and knowledgeable research organization it would be impossible to arrive at sound decisions on military questions in which the technical factor exerts a major influence.
In the development of new equipment and new techniques we must work closely with Canadian industry as a whole. Awareness of this has led the government to authorize the defence research board to develop an extended program of defence research in industry with a primary view of building up and maintaining a more adequate level of defence research capacity. The Department of Defence Production will be co-operating with the defence research board in selecting the research objectives for this expanded defence industrial research program.
I should now like to refer to the decisions the government has taken recently with regard to the deterioration of the situation in Europe. Since the house adjourned in July the international situation, especially with regard to Europe, has been the cause of concern to all nations of the western alliance. The announcement by Premier Khrushchev that the Soviet union intended to sign a separate peace treaty with Eastern Germany, coupled with military preparations taken by the communists, has led Canada and her allies to make a serious study of the implications of the Soviet moves. The decision of the Soviet union to resume nuclear weapons testing, followed by the recent atomic explosions, leaves little doubt in our minds as to the threat that faces us today. The Soviet ambassador to Canada is quoted as saying that the purpose of the resumption of such tests is to "jolt the allies" into agreement on disarmament. He might have added that such agreement is to be on communist terms and communist terms alone.
Following the conference of foreign ministers of the United States, France, Great Britain and Germany, the NATO council met on August 8, and as a result of this meeting the members unanimously agreed to consider measures they might take to bolster the overall NATO forces. Although Canada has lived up to her commitment to NATO in the past, the Canadian government after fully considering the matter decided to take certain action to further strengthen our contribution in Europe, and at the same time to increase the effectiveness of the forces committed to NATO in Canada and to step up the national survival program. Although announcements have already been made in this regard it would, I think, be useful to give a general summary at this time.

In so far as our national survival program is concerned, it has been decided to partially man emergency headquarters and warning centres in Canada; to stockpile and disperse certain stores; to accelerate the purchase of national survival equipment; to speed up the nuclear detonation and fall-out reporting system; to expedite the warning siren program and the survey of existing fall-out protection; and to carry out, as the Prime Minister said earlier, a national survival exercise later this fall to test the effectiveness of the program as a whole.
With their present strengths the regular army and the militia cannot supply the necessary personnel required as a result of the increased activity in the national survival program. To improve this position the government has approved a plan to increase, in the shortest possible time, the number of people trained to take part in survival and rescue operations should the need arise. It has been decided to train up to 100,000 men in the militia on special courses, each lasting six weeks. Approximately 25,000 will be trained on each course in existing military armouries across the country. As an example, training in the eastern Ontario area will not be limited to Ottawa but will be conducted also in Cornwall, Pembroke, Kingston, Peterborough, etc., all the places where military armouries exist and there is sufficient enrolment to justify a course.
Emphasis throughout will be on the teaching of subjects essential for national survival. There will be sufficient basic military training to provide the discipline and response essential to the control and effective employment of such a force on operations. Recruits will be trained with regular militia units in their home districts, and on completion of their courses will be given an opportunity to remain with the militia.
All trainees will be enrolled on a continuous call-out basis during the period of their course. They will receive normal pay with subsistance allowance in lieu of rations as given to a regular army recruit private of single status, that is $108 a month pay and a subsistence allowance of $65 per month. Standards of enrolment will be somewhat modified to permit acceptance of applicants between the ages of 18 and 50 years, married or single. Physical requirements based on the pulhems profile will not be as stringent as those now in force for the regular army.
The first course is scheduled to get under way before mid-November. For each course of 25,000 a training staff of approximately 2,700 officers and N.C.O.'s will be required. This staff will be found through existing instructional staff for the army survival
Supply-National Defence operations and from militia officers and N.C.O.'s and former regular army personnel called out on a voluntary basis for the duration of the program. Any deficiencies which may exist after calling on these three sources will be made up from the regular army. The administration of the program will be based on the existing militia structure.
In so far as our commitment to NATO is concerned, we are determined to make it perfectly clear that we fully support that organization. Over the past few years we have been strengthening the brigade group in Europe by modernizing and increasing the quantities of the brigade weapons. As an example, the armoured component of the brigade has been increased from squadron to regimental strength. Despite the increase in weapons and equipment, it was not considered necessary to make a corresponding increase in manpower. However, in a period of tension, and of course this is a period of tension, it is necessary to provide additional personnel to units in the field to ensure that they can, without delay, meet all their commitments on a 24-hour basis. The retention in the brigade of the first battalion of the Black Watch has already been announced. It is now proposed to strengthen the brigade group in Germany by the immediate addition of 1,100 men, of whom 300 are being allocated to man the surface to surface Honest John missile battery and to operate the reconnaissance helicopters which are being added to the brigade group.

Agreed.

I should like to thank the committee, Mr. Chairman. Initially the men to meet these requirements will be provided from existing units now in Canada. 1 might say that the first 400 men to strengthen the brigade will sail for Europe on the 22nd of this month, to be followed by a further 400 about a week later.
The strength of the R.C.A.F. air division in Europe is to be increased by 250 men. This will provide, amongst other things, an increased ratio of pilots to aircraft, thus improving the operational readiness of the division. In so far as the Royal Canadian Navy is concerned, we have a commitment to NATO for the provision of ships and aircraft in the event of an emergency. Our ships are at present manned at an average of 86 per cent of full operational complement. It is intended that immediate action be taken toward manning all operational ships at full

Supply-National Defence strength. This means the addition of some
1.750	personnel in naval strength.
A further decision has been made to increase the air transport capability of the R.C.A.F. It was planned that with the introduction of the long range Yukon aircraft, the North Star transport aircraft would be phased out of service. However, a squadron of these aircraft is now to be retained, thus enhancing the long range operations of air transport command. The extra manpower required involves some 500 personnel. To man the Pine Tree radar sites being transferred from the United States to Canada during the next few months without reducing other activities being undertaken by the R.C.A.F., an additional 490 personnel will be needed.
As a result of the increased manpower requirements, authority has been given to raise the strength ceilings of our forces in Europe from 12,000 to 14,000, and of the regular forces as a whole from 120,000 to 135,000.
I have already referred to the R.C.N. and R.C.A.F. requirement and the increase in strength of the fourth brigade group in Europe. In addition, it is proposed to maintain an immediate reserve of 1,500 men in Canada for the fourth brigade group, who will be available for immediate dispatch, with their documentation and so on, completed, to strengthen the strategic reserve forces of the army earmarked for NATO and to provide additional army personnel for national survival operations. Immediate steps are therefore being taken to recruit an additional
1.750	personnel for the R.C.N., some 11,600 for the Canadian army, and 1,140 for the R.C.A.F.
The estimated cost of these programs in round figures during the current fiscal year is $6 million for the survival measures, plus $25 million for the special militia training of men to take part in survival and rescue operations, and $12 million for the additions to the regular forces including the strengthening of the NATO forces overseas. Part of this cost can be met from the estimates now before the house. The net addition to defence spending when all adjustments have been taken into account will be in the order of $35 million. A question was asked the other day as to what the cost would be in a full year. The estimated cost of the measures I have mentioned for the year 1962-63 will be $62.9 million. For subsequent years it will be $55.3 million.
I should emphasize that the action we have taken should not be construed as indicating an alarmist attitude or any belief in the inevitability of war. Rather it indicates our recognition of the present critical international


situation, our belief in NATO, and our determination not to succumb to the threat of force no matter how awful that threat may appear. By taking such an attitude in consort with our allies it is our belief that the chances of war are diminished. It is not we who have resorted to sabre rattling and military threats. Premier Khrushchev has deliberately chosen to make an issue of the Berlin situation, has threatened the use of force unless we come to agreement on his terms, and has ignored the welfare of millions of people by resuming nuclear weapons testing. In the face of such threats of our national security, I think the committee will agree that the steps taken by the government are fully justified.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that some hon. members will be a bit disappointed, as I was, in the minister's statement. After commencing with a lecture to persons unnamed for spending too much time in discussing military hardware and not sufficient time in discussing over-all defence policy, he then proceeded to do just that. In fact his statement was a rehash of departmental administration, of many of the bits of information already contained in the blue book, and of the announcements made the other day by the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence. The statement contained very little, if anything, which was new or of interest to the committee.
I presume, Mr. Chairman, that although it was stated in different terms today by the minister, the objective of Canada's defence policy is still, as it has been in the past, to be an instrument of our foreign policy. It should be, therefore, organized for and dedicated to the maintenance of peace rather than the waging of thermonuclear war. Because of our relatively small population and military capacity, we must continue to work with the other members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization to achieve our goal. Our interdependence is such that we must consider western strength and capability as a whole before we can intelligently discuss what contribution Canada should be making to collective security; because, as the minister stated, we each make a contribution and the total strength of the alliance is equal to the sum of the individual contributions.
The struggle between the east and the west has been described as a protracted conflict. Not only is it protracted but the spectrum of the conflict is very broad, including competition in the economic, psychological, political and military spheres. Generally speaking, and subject only to a few happy exceptions, the west has been lagging in the various areas of conflict except its ability to deter an all-out,

direct thermonuclear attack. Even here the Russians have been narrowing the gap. They do not have the offensive power of the United States, but they are catching up. In addition, the fact that in a direct attack the Russians would strike first adds an equalizing factor to the deterrent equation.
The United States, realizing that in order to deter direct attack it must have the capacity to accept the first blow and still have enough potential to inflict unacceptable damage on the Soviet union, has embarked on a accelerated program designed to increase the invulnerability of its atomic striking force. They have embarked on a number of measures to achieve this goal. First of all, there is the Polaris submarine missile capacity. This is probably the most effective measure yet undertaken because the submarine, even though its location may be known at one moment, can hide from Soviet detection; and the deterrent capacity which it contains, and it is a very real deterrent capacity, is not vulnerable to Soviet attack.
In addition, the United States has embarked on an acceleration of the Minuteman program. As is known to the committee, this is a solid fuel intercontinental ballistic missile which will be installed in well dispersed hardened sites and later will be placed on mobile railroad cars so that its whereabouts will be unknown to any potential enemy. Then, too the Skybolt missile program has been accelerated. This is an air to ground missile with a relatively long range of 1,000 miles or so. It too is a solid fuel nuclear ballistic missile which carries an atomic warhead. It is to be carried by the B-52 bomber and by the British V bombers. Additionally, the United States has increased its capacity for an airborne alert and also its capacity for the 15 minute ground alert.
All these accelerated programs, Mr. Chairman, have been designed to make sure, to underline, the effectiveness of the United States to deter aggression, to deter a strike from the Soviet union. They have also improved their warning system. This is necessary if a ground alert is to be effective. As is well known, the first part of the ballistic missile early warning system is in operation, and the other parts will get into operation shortly. The Midas satellite system has been accelerated, and it is designed to provide a greater warning, perhaps of the order of 30 minutes, to the United States strategic air command.
All these steps combined increase the protection of the United States striking force and its ability to deter Soviet attack. I can say from experience, Mr. Chairman, having seen something of the strategic air command and of the steps it is taking, that it still has
Supply-National Defence an overwhelming capacity. It is formidable.
I know it has the capacity to blow the Soviet union off the face of the map. I think the Soviet union, too, is aware of this. I am convinced also the United States has and will keep its retaliatory forces up to date. They will not allow them to become out of date, and they will disperse them and make them invulnerable to attack as they feel required to do.
While Russia has been making giant strides toward narrowing the gap between its striking capacity and that of the United States, the west has been much slower in applying itself to the much greater gap between its conventional capacity and that of the Soviet union. The west does not have an adequate deterrent to moderate provocation. It does not have the conventional non-nuclear capacity to deter limited wars. Many people have been pointing out this inadequacy for some time. First of all, some of the more enlightened military officers did so. In most cases theirs was a minority opinion. When General Maxwell Taylor of the United States proposed this viewpoint it was considered radical and probably not correct. Now, at long last, this viewpoint is being accepted in official circles, and the United States has taken official notice of the deficiency in conventional strength and has included some remedial action in its current crash program.
President Kennedy stated the case well in his special message to congress on March 28, 1961. At that time he said:
The strength and deployment of our forces in combination with those of our allies should be sufficiently powerful and mobile to prevent the steady erosion of the free world through limited wars: and it is this role that should constitute the primary mission of our overseas forces. Non-nuclear wars, and sub-limited or guerrilla warfare, have since 1945 constituted the most active and constant threat to free world security. Those units of our forces which are stationed overseas, or designed to fight overseas, can be most usefully oriented toward deterring or confining those conflicts which do not justify and must not lead to a general nuclear attack. In the event of a major aggression that could not be repulsed by conventional forces, we must be prepared to take whatever action with whatever weapons are appropriate. But our objective now is to increase our ability to confine our response to non-nuclear weapons, and to lessen the incentive for any limited aggression by making clear what our response will accomplish. In most areas of the world, the main burden of local defence against overt attack, subversion and guerrilla warfare must rest on local populations and forces. But given the great likelihood and seriousness of this threat, we must be prepared to make a substantial contribution in the form of strong, highly mobile forces trained in this type of warfare, some of which must be deployed in forward areas, with a substantial airlift and sealift capacity and prestocked overseas bases.
The President backed up his policy statement by action with specific recommendations

Supply-National Defence to implement the policy. These included the following, and I may say that the lettering is my own:
A.	Expanded research on non-nuclear weapons. I hope the President:
What is needed are entirely new types of nonnuclear weapons and equipment with increased firepower, mobility and communications, and more suited to the kind of tasks our limited war forces will most likely be required to perform.
B.	Increased airlift capacity. The appropriation put before congress was more than double the existing appropriation.
C.	Additional amphibious transport to increase the speed and capability of sealift capacity.
D.	Helicopters, rifles, electronics and communications equipment.
E.	Development of an advanced tactical fighter emphasizing non-nuclear capabilities.
F.	Modification of the F-105 tactical fighter to improve its capability to handle conventional armament ordnance items and to increase its suitability for airstrips of all types of areas.
G.	More personnel and training.
This new emphasis on increasing western capacity to deter or if necessary wage limited war is a complete vindication of the change in direction suggested by the Liberal party in this house a year ago. President Kennedy's recommendations in March, 1961, read like a catalogue of the suggestions we put forward as a consequence of a redirected policy.
He must have read them.

I think he did so. I feel it is unfortunate that the Canadian government has not yet seen the light. Now that we have a new Berlin crisis on our hands we see some evidence of token repentance. We hope it is not deathbed repentance. Now at the insistent urging of its allies the Canadian government is sending token reinforcements to its brigade group and air division in Europe. One might wonder what additional contributions we were asked to make. One might wonder about the connection between our lack of ground forces in Europe and the Berlin crisis.
Our lack of conventional strength there is well known to Mr. Khrushchev. It is also well known to Mr. Khrushchev that as the common market is enlarged, and as it becomes stronger, Europe is gaining in strength politically, economically and militarily. He also knows that finally the western allies have agreed to build up their conventional strength in Europe. Taking all these factors into consideration, he may have decided that now is the strategic time to cause trouble and see how far he can press without running


into absolute opposition from the NATO alliance. However, if we had been stronger on the ground in Europe the crisis might never have arisen in the first place.
The government has announced that 1,106 additional troops will be sent to our brigade in Europe. It has indicated that 300 of these will man the Honest John artillery.

I beg the minister's pardon. We have not been told what the remainder will be occupied in doing. We would ask the government to tell us specifically what function they will perform, and how in fact they add to the fighting effectiveness of the brigade in Europe. We concur in that decision, but we deplore the failure of the government to provide modern equipment for the brigade. It has not been supplied with the mobility and firepower it needs. This is the situation notwithstanding the minister's brave words in many of the speeches he has made across the country. It has none of the light aircraft which are available such as the Otter, Beaver, and Caribou. Other armies have them, even other armies in Europe. However, the Canadian army has none of them.
On recent trips to the United States, visiting their army installations, it has been a matter of pride that the United States army relies to the extent it does on the excellent series of light aircraft manufactured by the de Havilland company in Toronto. United States army personnel just naturally assume that the Canadian army would be well equipped with these first class Canadian products. They can scarcely believe that such is not the case. Indeed, they are not the only incredulous ones. On one recent trip three of my Conservative colleagues also could not believe that the Canadian army would not be equipped with the Caribou aircraft. They were reluctant to take my word for it, but they accepted information supplied by a Canadian liaison officer. It is humiliating, Mr. Chairman, that we have such excellent equipment available but not available where it is needed, in the field with our forces.
As a sidelight here I might be permitted to say that this trip to which I was just referring was one during which parliamentarians of the NATO countries visited United States installations as guests of the United States congress and government. It was a most fascinating as well as instructive trip. We visited installations of the marine corps, the army, the navy and the air force. We saw a fairly wide spectrum of United States installations, and were given an insight into their capacity and plans. I should like to say for myself-and I am sure I speak for

my colleagues on the other side of the house as well, including Mr. Chairman-that we appreciated the courtesy which was extended to us, as well as the hospitality. The Americans are wonderfully hospitable people. They treated us with great respect and great deference and made the trip as instructive, pleasant and congenial as possible. We are extremely grateful to them for the opportunity that was presented to us.
Similarly, our army has not been equipped with helicopters. Goodness knows the suggestion has been made often enough. As found in Hansard at page 7525 for August 3, 1960, the then minister of national defence-and I join the present minister in his tribute to the former minister, who was a special friend of mine and a man for whom I had the greatest respect-Hon. George Pearkes had this to say, referring to the recommendations of the special committee on defence expenditures:
The committee also recommended giving consideration to the provision of helicopters which would increase the mobility of the brigade. We have that matter under consideration and it is just a question of when funds are to be made available, because I believe that helicopters will certainly increase the effectiveness of that brigade.
The army itself seems to be enthusiastic about the idea of obtaining helicopters. I quote part of a dispatch from camp Gage-town, New Brunswick, by Dave McIntosh, dated July 11, as follows:
The army wants some 40 of these helicopters and 40 transport types, but the government has not yet approved expenditure of the some $40 million required for this purpose.
It is true that some light reconnaissance helicopters are included in this year's estimates, but to my knowledge there is no provision for the heavier transport types which are required for moving troops and equipment on the battlefield.
So it is also with the personnel carrier. The Bobcat program has been slowed to a crawl. Instead of being accelerated and providing the desperately needed equipment to our brigade group, the government has done its best, and its best has been pretty good, to postpone necessary expenditures for budgetary reasons. The same story applies to a broad band of needed requirements; no money, no equipment. No money, that is, for the most important equipment. Some has been found for less useful projects.
The point is that the armed forces are starved for the type of equipment they require to do an effective job. It is a matter of regret and of deep concern that the appropriation for equipment for this fiscal year is the smallest since the post-Korean build up. It has been said that we have the best clothed
Supply-National Defence and best fed forces in the world. It is not possible to say that their equipment is the latest or the best. We were told by the minister in his statement today that it should be; that their equipment should be second to none, but the fact is that their equipment is not the best. It is second and inferior to equipment they might face in the hands of their enemy.
Now we are advised that the armed forces are to be augmented by approximately 15,000 men of all ranks, but there is no corresponding increase in the appropriation for equipment. On the contrary, one wonders how the new personnel can be paid with the funds referred to by the minister. He has told us that only $35 million will be required for the balance of the year. According to the blue book the cost of military personnel for 1961-62, including operations and maintenance, is approximately $10,000 per man. On a proportional basis, therefore, the annual cost of
15.000	additional men would be $150 million, and that is before any allowance is provided for equipment. As more than six months remain of the fiscal year, either the government does not expect its new program to be very effective or it has not made adequate financial provision.
There is also the cost of training the
100.000	civil survival recruits and providing equipment for them. I will leave further discussion of this subject until later. In passing however, Mr. Chairman, I might say that I agree with the minister's statement today that there remains a lot to be done. His was the understatement of the year.
Our whole concern here is one of direction. The government is not putting proper emphasis on developing mobile forces capable of assisting in the deterrence of limited war or, in the event one should be waged, of containing it before it spreads into a major conflagration. It continues to place far too great an emphasis on weapons systems which are not needed to deter direct attack, which do nothing to deter limited war, and which are relatively useless in the event of an all-out war. The minister said in Toronto:
Here in North America the major component of the threat to this continent is still the manned bomber regardless of what many of our so-called experts are claiming.
I would refer the minister to a book entitled "War and Peace in the Space Age" written by Lieutenant General James M. Gavin, who has this to say:
In conclusion, in the missile-space age the earth will become a tactical theatre, and combat in space will have begun. Missiles will be the dominant form of firepower and air mobility will provide the key to tactical success in land warfare. Through air mobility we must discover the innovations that will give us the margin of advantage we need to win in land combat.
