Supply-National Defence
When will that happen?

If Lieutenant General Gavin is correct, the minister is wrong on two counts. First of all the Prime Minister has told this house the missile is replacing the manned bomber as the main threat. The minister is now living in that unenlightened era of about four years ago. Second, if air mobility is needed in the field, the minister is missing the boat because his troops do not have any; and according to most of the experts, including Lieutenant General Gavin, they require it. I should like the minister to give more reasons why he and his government have delayed so long in providing this essential equipment.
It is interesting to note that in the long list of priority items presented by President Kennedy to congress on March 28 last there did not appear one of the major items on which the Canadian government is relying. Not one American penny for the Voodoo, the F-104, the Bomarc or the Honest John. The Canadian defence department has become a pawnshop for second hand American hardware.
Now we are being prepared for the introduction of atomic arms into Canada. The campaign to wear down the resistance in this house and in the country has begun. Speeches are being made by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of National Defence which lead us to believe that the introduction of these weapons is inevitable. The commander in chief of NORAD was brought to Toronto to make a speech which would frighten the Canadian people into submission. At this point, Mr. Chairman, I think I should raise the question of the propriety of the Canadian government asking General Kuter to come and make a speech designed to do the government's political chores. I think if the government has any policy in which it firmly believes, it should state the case and accept the responsibility without trying to palm it off on military officers.
Our position in this respect is the same as we announced last year. We still feel that atomic weapons in Canada are unnecessary at this time. We feel they are redundant. We do not think they add anything to the security of Canada, and we think they provide no protection for the strategic air command. In his speech at Toronto the minister gave as one of the reasons for continuing the expenditure of large sums of money on these weapons systems the fact that they provide some protection for the deterrent, for the retaliatory striking power of the United States strategic air command. This position was valid four years ago; it is not valid now. It was valid at


a time when the bomber was the only threat to the North American continent. It is no longer valid.
The present situation, as the minister knows and as he should be expounding instead of having it done for him, is that if the Russians were to start a war now; if they were to embark upon a direct attack, they would not do so unless they had enough missiles to cover every American strategic air command base on the North American continent. That is fundamental. It would be suicidal-it might be suicidal anyway-for the Soviet union to start a war even by sneak attack if they did not have sufficient missile capacity to wipe out every strategic air command base in the first hour or so of the conflict.
The United States understands this. That is the reason for the accelerated programs to which I referred earlier in my speech. That is the reason the United States is stepping up the Polaris program. That is the reason they are going to accelerate the Minuteman program and alert more strategic air command bombers. They know that 30 minutes after war starts any SAC aircraft which is not off the ground will not be able to get off the ground.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired. Will the committee give unanimous consent?
Agreed.

I thank the committee for its co-operation. The minister should understand the point I have just made. This is at the heart of the United States strategy now. They know they will not have time to call pilots in after a war has begun. The only thing they will have with which to strike back will be those components of the retaliatory force which are invulnerable in the event of attack by missile in the first few minutes of conflict.
The minister's strategy is four years old. He is still living in the "aircraft only" age. He has not projected himself into the missile age. Perhaps he has received some wrong advice from the department. If he has he should overcome it, because that is what he is paid for, and I hope he will do it without too much delay.
There is one element of the SAC retaliatory force I omitted to mention. If the hardened missile bases did not receive a direct blow within the first few minutes of attack they would have a period of two or three hours before any bombers would reach their location, during which time the missiles could be launched toward the Soviet union. If they were not launched in that period of time they would have no opportunity whatever.

This is the sum and substance of the United States strategy. Under these circumstances our Bomarc, even if it had any utility whatsoever, and our defence mechanisms other than warning and reconnaissance do not in fact protect the deterrent. They may do other things, but they do not accomplish this end.
For this reason we continue to believe that it is not worth while to put Canada into the atomic club, into the group of atomic nations, when the advantage of having atomic weapons on Canadian soil is so negligible. We reserve the right to reassess this position if at any time in the future the west should be successful in developing a really effective anti-missile missile. That would change the picture considerably. At the present time, however, there is none, and we are basing our policy on the facts as they exist.
In respect to atomic arms for NATO, our position there, too, is the same as that announced in this house last year. We believe that the first and primary emphasis should be on the building up of conventional strength in NATO, the building up of the capacity to deter limited aggression, and the building up of a flexible response. We believe this is the first priority. Second, we have taken the position that if atomic weapons of the defensive type are required as a second line of defence in NATO we would not object to Canadian forces being so equipped if these weapons came under NATO collective control. We take this position with the knowledge that if we had sufficient conventional strength to stop any Russian attack for days or weeks, there would be adequate time for consultation and for the decision to be made. The Leader of the Opposition, if he has an opportunity to participate in this debate, will elaborate on the political aspects of NATO co-operation and on the control of weapons within the NATO alliance.
In respect to our contribution to the United Nations, this party is proud of it. We are proud of the part our leader has played in making the United Nations a useful vehicle for international intervention. We hope that Canada's role in this field will increase. We hope that the usefulness of the United Nations in settling and arbitrating international disagreements will increase. We believe that we in Canada should support and build up those types of mobile tactical forces which are most effective for that type of job. This is the policy we put forward.
I shall leave until later the discussion of the role of the individual services and some of the equipment items that have been ordered for them. I feel that they can be better dealt with when the specific relevant items have been called.
Supply-National Defence
The whole purpose of the change of direction which has been suggested from this side of the house is to increase the effectiveness of Canada's contribution. We know we have to remain a member of the alliance. We know that the alliance is only as strong as the sum total of all contributions of the member nations. We do not think the Canadian contribution at the present time is adding very much to that collective strength. We feel that by a change in direction and by placing greater emphasis on the deficits in our collective strength we can make a much greater and more useful contribution.
There are side benefits, as well. There is the benefit of using in most cases equipment which can be designed and manufactured in this country, which will provide employment for Canadian workers. But this aside, the real purpose of our policy and the reason we urge a reconsideration on the government is this. We feel the government should stop wasting its money on Bomarc missiles and ten year old concepts. We urge it to enter the missile age, to accept the facts as they exist, and to attempt to make Canada's contribution to collective defence a useful and constructive one.

Mr. Chairman, it is with considerable trepidation that I rise at this point to participate in this debate. The committee will realize that my participation is due to the absence of the hon. member for Vancouver East. I am sure all hon. members of the committee join me in wishing him the best of health and in trusting that he will soon recover and resume his place in this chamber.
I am aware that members of the opposition are at the greatest disadvantage in discussing the question of national defence and related subjects. Naturally there is available to the minister information which cannot be made available to those on the opposition benches. I therefore think it behoves us on this side of the house to perhaps apologize in advance if through misinformation or lack of information we should be led to say anything which on the basis of the minister's knowledge is grossly unfair and which, because of the requirement of secrecy, he is unable to answer.
Although, as I have said, I rise with trepidation and some concern, I am heartened by a statement attributed to a United States defence strategist, Mr. Walter Millis, who said:
The ablest students of the subject are either in complete contradiction or in a state of frank bewilderment.

Like the last speaker.

Supply-National Defence

I am not commenting on the interjection which has just been made by an hon. gentleman on my left.
This is the first opportunity the house has had to discuss the question of life and death in relation to the problem of national defence. There is no problem which appears to generate more emotion. There is no subject in respect to which clear, cold logic is more necessary. I think many of us sitting here will agree that the differences of opinion are not between those who are loyal and those who are disloyal; rather the division is as to how this loyalty and love of country can be best expressed. It is not a difference between those who want war and those who want peace. We on this side of the house are fully confident that those who sit to the right of the Speaker's chair are as determined for and as desirous of peace as we are, but rather there is a serious difference regarding how war may come in the 1960's and the kind of war it will be. Although we on this side speak a great deal of peace we do not stand with a great moral case and look down upon those who are seeking peace in other ways. That is not the difference in any way. We believe wholeheartedly in the good intentions of all hon. members.
Third, it is not a difference between those who are pro-American and those who are anti-American; rather we may have two views on how we can best be the allies of the United States of America. Surely, Mr. Chairman, it is not a debate in which such words as "pacifism" or "neutralism" have any place, because it is not a difference of neutralism versus active alliance; rather it is a difference as to by what form of international participation-"participation" is a word which I think all parties in the house accept-Canada can best make a contribution.
As I stand here I recognize that men of all parties have played an active role in the fighting for freedom which has taken place in this century; therefore this is a question on which the motives of all hon. members should never be questioned. We have all wanted a peaceful world. We may be divided on the means by which this peace can be obtained.
There are many approaches to the subject of preventing war. No doubt the most popular one is the historical argument-and it is a very telling argument in so many ways-that if we had maintained our alliances, if we had kept our weapons in the 1930's, we would have prevented the march into the Rhineland, and we would have prevented the march into Austria, Czechoslovakia and Poland. If we had kept our weapons we could have stopped world war II and the world

would have been saved from the scourge of universal conflict. This is always a very popular concept, that history repeats itself; that we can avoid the mistakes of the past by heeding the warnings of the past.
Well, one historian has been very cynical, and has said that the only thing we learn from history is that we do not learn anything from history; but I think we can learn a great deal from history as long as we do not try to force patterns which do not exist; because the irony of mankind's story is that history never repeats itself.
The belief in the 1920's and 1930's was that if the world forsook arms it would be another way of finding peace. We believed that if we had set up a League of Nations we would have stopped world war I. In the 1920's and 1930's we would have stopped world war I but we failed to stop world war II. The difference is that in the 1960's it is quite possible that our policies may be directed at stopping world war II, but the dreadful question is whether it will stop world war III. Indeed, an aroused America and the presence of weapons in the 1930's would have prevented the march of Hitler but the problem, of course, remains, what are we to do in 1961? We may hope that the solution of the 1930's will stop us from the wars of the 1960's, but I have not quite that great confidence that it will; because we exist in a new world of new weaponry, of new patterns of events, and only new solutions will have any effect upon those patterns of events.
Just briefly I should like to quote from Sir John Cockcroft, who said in 1957:
It is clear enough already, however, that our civilization can be destroyed in a night-
Probably it can be said at this time that our civilization can be destroyed in a few minutes. I continue:
It is clear enough already, however, that our civilization can be destroyed in a night if ever these great forces are released for our destruction. This presents the human race with the greatest challenge it has ever had: to co-operate in disarmament and so to banish the threat which now hangs over the whole world.
I realize, of course, that this government has played a great part in its attempt to bring about disarmament. This is a problem which we face. I think our defence policies and our external affairs policies must be dovetailed, must indeed be the same, and that anything which takes place in defence must in no way compromise or interfere with what is taking place in the Department of External Affairs in preventing war; because surely this is the end of our defence policy. A former minister of national defence said in this house last year that the primary aim of our defence policy must be not to win war but to prevent war. He certainly would be supported by

General MacArthur who said that it is a form of mutual suicide, and the entire effort of modern society should be concentrated on an endeavour to outlaw it.
Will you call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, when we adjourned for lunch at one o'clock I had opened my remarks by suggesting that the end of defence policy is always the same for all parties. The security of the Canadian people, security of life and property and also, as the Minister of National Defence pointed out this morning, freedom of the Canadian people. We are as concerned with the quality of life as we are concerned with life itself. I attempted to point out that no defence policy can be found in 1961 by looking at the past, by assuming that we can stop a third world war by means by which we could have stopped world war II because, as one great historian and theologian, Reinhold Niebuhr, has put it, this is the irony of human history. It is not that we wish war; it is simply that we cannot make the intellectual jump to keep us sufficiently ahead of events to prevent a new pattern from emerging which will bring war while we are trying to decide on how to deal with the older pattern.
So too in respect of weaponry we have become enamoured of the weaponry of the past. As the hon. member for Trinity suggested this morning, we are four years behind and perhaps in our basic concepts we are even further behind. A look at past wars will convince us that the first few months of every war have been fought with the weapons of the preceding war. We tried cavalry in world war I and the Maginot line in world war II, and we are still trying to defend against manned bombers in 1961. In spite of the fact that manned bombers are certainly the most accurate form of attack, none the less these are not the weapons which in my opinion will be used in any war which might begin within the next few years. Indeed, I understand that the accuracy of the long range missiles which the Russians are developing was such as to mean a degree of error of two or three miles, but that margin of error has been cut down tremendously over the last number of months. So in a real way we are bound by the past and we even talk about past events, but so far as an all-out war in defence of the North American continent is
Supply-National Defence concerned there is no defence. We are confusing the word "defence" with the word "deterrent", and we in Canada can play virtually no role in the realm of deterrence.
No more can we talk of winning the war. This is entirely irrational. I think the Minister of National Defence was quite right this morning when he said that we should not be motivated by fear, but I think we should be basing our defence on a realistic and rational realization of what the stakes really are and what kind of war we are really going to be fighting. I think it is rather important to know that each of the 16 missiles on each of the five Polaris submarines has more power than all the bombs dropped during the last war.
There seems to be a peculiar notion in some circles that this is going to be a limited nuclear war and that only a certain number of bombs which we know Russia and the United States have will be dropped, but surely this is a strange strategic concept. Surely when this war begins it will have to be an all-out war for the first few seconds. All the power of the opposing side will have to be destroyed; because if this is not done the subsequent attack by the opposing power will be such that it will bring about certainly most unacceptable damage to the country which originally launched the attack.
The United States has suggested that one and a half thousand megatons dropped on the United States would kill 49 million people, with only 263 bombs dropped. We know that the U.S.S.R. has 20,000 megatons capable of being dropped on the United States, and only
9,000	would be needed to wipe out all life. These are only a few statistics, but I think we should all know the stakes not in order to increase fear but in order to know exactly what we can do in this kind of situation.
Not only is it impossible to compare the policies of the past and the lessons of the past, but it is irrelevant to compare the role which Canada can play. In world war I Canada played a magnificent role in the forefront of the western front; indeed, she was the pride of the western front. In world war II we played an extremely important role, not as dramatic but as valuable. In world war III we will find ourselves in a world of two giants and we, as one author has put it, will be peeping between the legs of these giants. We will virtually have no role whatever. In other words, to put it in the vernacular, we are out of this league. We should therefore try to ascertain where we can best make a valuable contribution to the peace of the world.
It was in recognition of these facts, that we can no longer expect the old weapons will be used or that our role will necessarily be

Supply-National Defence as it was in the past, that the New Democratic party has tried to base its belief once again on a defence policy that will guard the life and property of the Canadian people as well as the freedoms and liberties of the Canadian people. It must be a policy which will take into account the uniqueness of our present situation.
We stand on two premises. The first is that we should do nothing in defence which will limit our activities in the area of diplomacy in seeking out a real peace. Yesterday the Prime Minister talked of the Secretary of State for External Affairs as the idealist. We in this corner feel the minister is a realist in terms of the kind of world in which we live. He is determined that war will not take place; and that must be our basic policy, to prevent war. It makes it very difficult for us to be enthusiastic proponents of disarmament if we accept nuclear arms or if we are so two faced about it that the other countries do not know whether or not we are accepting them. We cannot fight to limit the nuclear club, so to speak, to those who have the weapons now if we give any indication that we wish to join the nuclear club. We have heard of the big threat in the production of atomic weapons whereby countries, perhaps 25 in the world, will be able to arm themselves with these weapons. This is the area in which Canada must make a real contribution, to keep nuclear weapons out of the hands of more nations. It is for this reason I suggest our defence policy must in no way compromise the activities of our diplomats in this cause.
The second premise on which we have based our policy is that Canada is a middle power in size, in population and in opportunities. We cannot, like Stephen Leacock's hero, jump on a horse and ride off in all directions. We feel it is not possible for us to go in even one direction. But we feel that by going in too many directions we could lose all direction. I think the Minister of National Defence would agree with this proposition, that at certain times it might mean more to the security of the life and property, to the security of the freedom of the Canadian people, if we were feeding the people of southeast Asia rather than providing a certain kind of missile. It is for this reason we say that our participation must be a directed participation, not a directionless participation; one that has possibilities for Canada as a middle power.
As we have said, the significant fact is that the really big league defence is the deterrent. The deterrent has reached the area of the overkill. We have heard some interesting information this morning about the extent to which our friends south of the border have

been carrying on their program of deterrents. Canada can play no vital role in deterrents.
The problem is, where can we play a significant role? We believe that this area is the field of foreign aid. We can play an important role here, and we must not allow our activities in the area of deterrents to destroy that role.
This morning the minister used a very interesting example. He said we should not wait until the bear is ready to attack before we buy a rifle. We would all question the sanity of any person who waited until the bear was ready to attack before he bought a rifle. We would also question the sanity of a person who made no decision about shells when he bought the rifle. This situation exists in Canada today. We do not know what the shells are going to be in terms of this rifle. We are told that the weapons we have bought are practically useless without nuclear warheads, the reference being to the Bomarc and the CF-104.
Well, is it possible that we are waiting to let propaganda, to let the effect of the weapons themselves, make the decision for us? Are we going to have a clear-cut position taken by this government, one which can be debated in this house; because it will be clearly impossible to debate the possibility of acquiring nuclear weapons when the time arrives. There will be no time to discuss or debate the subject at that time. Of course the whole example breaks down badly. A better example might be that of a person who buys a bottle of nitroglycerine to throw at the bear so he can blow himself up and the bear at the same time. One cannot claim to compare nuclear weapons with a rifle in terms of a war.
We believe, then, that there are three kinds of war. The first is one which will start by mistake, and that is why we are wholeheartedly behind the activities of the man we refer to as a realist, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in his attempt to continue efforts at disarmament. Second, there is the war that might be started by the two great powers. If this war comes I seriously doubt whether Canada will have any part to play whatever. It seems inconceivable to me that the decisions which will have to be made in consequence will provide time for consultation with the NATO allies, and particularly Canada. It will require secretiveness in terms of manning the submarines, the intercontinental ballistic missiles and so on, to such an extent that this war will be decided by a very few men on a very limited part of the earth's surface.
As this debate goes on we would hope to have the opportunity of looking at this blue book of national defence in the light of a

possible nuclear war between the great powers and seeing what these deficiencies are. This is something which will be carried on if this debate continues. We can detect, with the D.E.W. line and reconnaissance aircraft, but we do not feel that the D.E.W. line and this reconnaissance is necessarily a part of our NORAD arrangements.
But there is a way in which Canada can make a real contribution in terms of a limited war, the bind of war which has been breaking out so often. Since the end of the second world war there have been some 30 of these limited wars. We have many young nations arriving on the scene. All of us know that during the first years of nationalism, aggressive tendencies very often come to the fore. This is the area in which we feel the defence policy of Canada can play a part. We should have a mobile force capable of taking police action in other areas of the world where these situations might arise.
We feel there should be a reappraisal of Canada's defence policy, a reappraisal of the determination to prevent war.
We feel that we must leave NORAD. We feel we should have an expanded foreign aid program. We have suggested 2 per cent of the gross national product, not because we are being unrealistic in terms of Canada's possibilities but because we are trying to be realistic in terms of the need. This need has been mentioned by the Associate Minister of National Defence and other members, notably the hon. member for Greenwood. We want to cut down in our defence expenditures in areas where we feel there is waste in terms in the kind of war which Canada will be undertaking if the possibilities should materialize. It is rather frightening to realize that in the cost of war, or of preparing for war, mankind is spending at least $120 billion a year. If we could spend that amount on peace we could bring up the income of each person in China, India and Pakistan. We could double their income. We could provide adequate housing for 240 million people in underdeveloped nations. We could give the three billion hungry people food and medical care.

No, that is not what I am advocating. I suggested that we should be selecting areas where we are playing no part whatsoever. I think the Bomarc missile is a very good example of an area where we could
Supply-National Defence very well be spending something on foreign aid. We have suggested no nuclear weapons on Canadian soil.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: May I ask a further question for the purpose of clarification? I understand that our expenditures for Bomarc bases run in the area of $15 million. Is that the amount of change the hon. member is advocating, or is he advocating some greater change?

I have been advocating a change in other areas, but I have certainly not suggested the disbanding of the military forces. If the hon. member will wait until I have finished I am sure that position will become evident.
We suggested there should be no nuclear weapon on Canadian soil because it adds nothing to deterrence. It does not defend us, and we lose immeasurably in our moral force. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said that we must have faith and courage. This is an area where possibly faith and courage will be very necessary.
I should like to read a short editorial or a short excerpt from an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of May 4, 1961:
Canada's two Bomarc bases will be ready within a few months to launch their missiles against hostile bombers. During this interval we can expect increasing pressure to tip the Bomarcs with nuclear warheads. Proof of this pressure is found in parliamentary debates like that on Tuesday when the external affairs minister, Mr. Howard Green, said a decision to acquire nuclear warheads depended on progress that is made in the next few months toward disarmament... Already the defence minister, Mr. Douglas Harkness, has declared that the full potential of Bomarc launching sites cannot be attained without nuclear warheads.
Lieutenant General Robert M. Lee, vice commander of United States air defence command, having no need to worry about elections, has stated flatly that Canada's two Bomarc bases are useless without atomic warheads.
He also goes on to point out the seriousness of any such stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member would give the date of that quotation.

Yes, the date was May 4, 1961. The heading of the editorial is "Ban the A-Bomarc".
I have here an editorial which appeared in the Toronto daily Star of May 11, 1961:
The nuclear arms now being considered by the Canadian government are warheads for the Bomarc anti-aircraft missile. The Bomarcs are for use against manned H-bombers-a declining threat. They are useless against intercontinental missiles.
"They will contribute precisely nothing to our safety in the event of a nuclear war," says Maj. Gen. W. H. S. Macklin, former adjutant general of the Canadian army ...
Our obvious interest is to do all that a middle power can do to prevent a general holocaust. Renunciation of nuclear weapons would serve that

Supply-National Defence end, whereas acceptance of them would sabotage the crusade of external affairs minister Green for world disarmament.
I think that is a position which we in this party can accept. We also accept the suggestion of the development of a brigade of troops which we can keep in areas where limited wars are taking place. I think we were all heartened by the suggestion of the Prime Minister yesterday and of the Leader of the Opposition the day before that this was a role for the United Nations. Would it not be extremely valuable if we could go to the United Nations session when it opens and suggest that we have a brigade ready to move to the Brandenburg gate, to take part in the guarding of the access roads or in the prevention of any activity there which might create a nuclear war? Would it not be worth while if we could join, possibly with a member from the eastern bloc or possibly with a member from the neutralist bloc, in providing those forces? We have done it previously and, as one person has put it, this was our finest hour at the United Nations. Is it not time that we began to work in that direction once again?
We were also interested in the remarks made by the Minister of National Defence with regard to the defence research board, and we shall be discussing some of the matters under that head as time goes on. Is it not time that we had a peace research institute, as suggested by a scientist in the Oakville area, Mr. Norman Alcock, within the Department of National Defence? So long as we have hundreds of men seeking to find methods of creating armaments and only a few in the area of disarmament dealing with peace, we have very little opportunity to bring the scientific approach to the area of peace as well as to that of war. Could it not be independent of our national government but subsidized by the national government and working along with the Department of National Defence and the Department of External Affairs?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I must advise the hon. member that his time has expired.
I thank the house very much for this opportunity. I shall be only one or two minutes more.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I should put on record the consent of the committee, if the hon. member does not mind. Does the committee give its unanimous consent to give the hon. member additional time?
Agreed.

For example, we are very much concerned about accidental war. Is

there no possibility that we could have scientists working in areas which would help us to provide a means of guarding against this happening? I think all of us have been concerned that at SAC headquarters there have been situations in which the screen detected something but they were not sure what it was, and it later turned out to be a flock of geese. We are concerned that such a very small thing might very well touch off a nuclear war. Could we not have some means of providing scientists with an opportunity of doing research into ways of stopping war, even in the area of psychology as well. We are concerned as to what effect disarmament would have on our economy. Surely a defence research board working for war could well be set off by a peace institute working for peace.
I have attempted to put forward a very general pattern of the New Democratic party's program in view of a new and frightening world and in view of the weapons of annihilation. Canada should not be fearful but rather should be determined to play a role in an area in which she can have some effect. We can do very little or virtually nothing in the area of deterrence of all-out war. We can play a role in deterring a limited war, in taking police action within the United Nations structure or of taking police action in such areas as Berlin; extending our foreign aid programs; a defence policy exhibiting our desire for peace and placing weapons for peace in the hands of those who are to seek peace at the negotiation tables of the world.
These are the hopes of all parties, that we can find a policy which will bring security and freedom to the people of Canada.
We certainly hope that the defence of our nation will be looked after with efficiency, but we are concerned even more that it should be looked after in the light of the new events, the new kind of world in which we live, and with the new policies which must be adopted.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with great care to the speeches which have been made during the initial stages of this debate, first of all by my colleague the Minister of National Defence, and then by the critic of the official opposition and my good friend the hon. member for Trinity. I have also listened with care to the most interesting speech just delivered in this committee by the hon. member for Peterborough. I should like, with your permission, Mr. Chairman, to start my remarks in French and then to continue in English.

Supply-National Defence (Translation):
First of all, I should like to tell members of the committee how much I have been considering myself privileged, since my appointment to the position I now occupy in the Department of National Defence, to serve with two highly distinguished colleagues.
I should like first to salute my excellent friend and colleague, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) who, after a remarkable military career, has added to his talents of a born politician those of a very competent administrator.
I should like also to salute the Hon. George Pearkes, who is now occupying the exalted functions of lieutenant governor of British Columbia. The Hon. Mr. Pearkes has also had a most remarkable military career. All those who are familiar with army life see in him the greatest contemporary Canadian soldier. As a cabinet member, he showed outstanding talents as a politician as well as an administrator. I know that he is carrying out very efficiently the important duties entrusted to him, and I wish him many years of happiness and great success in all his endeavours.
In the statement he made before the committee, the Minister of National Defence clearly defined the situation which is facing us. In the course of my remarks, I will try and avoid any unnecessary repetition of the arguments he put forward. I feel however that it might be useful to acquaint members of the committee with my personal views on military matters under review in this debate. I should also like to reply to the criticisms made by our learned friends of the opposition, concerning the military strategy and tactics used at this time by the Department of National Defence.
Mr. Chairman, it is most unfortunate that in 1961 we should still find it necessary to speak of defence and worry about events which are happening in a foreign land and which threaten us with a third world war. It would have been logical to think that after two horrible wars which tore our civilization and caused millions of deaths, countless sufferings and incalculable destruction, mankind would have come to realize that wars are useless and that it is only in peace that can be found progress, prosperity and salvation of future generations.
It would seem that the sacrifice of those who gave their lives on the battlefields of the world
where they fought with enthusiasm and conviction, should have been acknowledged with something else than the war threats which are hovering over the world today.
But we have to admit that mankind did not learn, and today more than at any time in its history, this earth of ours is threatened by the most terrifying cataclysm that be, a nuclear attack, if it should ever take place.
And yet, it seems that the ideal for which our fathers and brothers fought in two successive wars was an ideal of truth and justice. The various nations should have realized that happiness and our very civilization lie in the pursuit of that ideal. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, is there in the world anything more beautiful than this freedom we defended on the battlefield in two consecutive wars? Is there anything finer than this freedom of speech, of thought, of religion, of expression, this freedom to choose freely our own way?
Is there anything finer than freedom? How is it that half the world, instead of realizing the blessings of freedom, is now attempting to spread communist theories which can only lead civilization to the most unfortunate and cruel slavery.
Anyone who has travelled in the underdeveloped countries of the world realizes that this democracy in which we believe and our principles of life are the best, and that it is through the observance of those principles that we have succeeded in attaining our present standard of living which is rightly considered as the highest in the world today.
Those who appreciate the extent of our development should readily understand that happiness and progress are to be found under the democratic system and that they should give up these communist theories which, as I just said, can only bring chaos, confusion and disorder to the peoples of the world.
But let us face the sad facts: what we have to cope with in 1961 is a struggle between two ideals. Our ideal, the one which we feel is the only noble and fine one, is that of true democracy as we know it; our opponents' ideal is that of communist expansion throughout the world. Unfortunately, both sides have at their disposal extremely powerful weapons and we must live with- we come back on that point in each of our speeches and that thought is with us at every moment of the day-the possibility of this abominable catastrophe of a nuclear attack.
In the advent of a nuclear war, the aggressor would most definitely have an advantage.

Supply-National Defence It is obvious that if the attack is violent enough, he will be able to cause incalculable damage to the attacked country. Yet, on the other hand, the aggressor is not without knowing that practically as soon as he attacks there will be retaliation and that he will be destroyed and even wiped off the face of the earth. Therefore, nuclear war can only lead to the complete ruin of civilization, to the end of the world.
It is indeed because of the sheer horror of such a possibility that we find some comfort despite the problem facing us. We do believe that mankind will not agree to exterminate itself; but rather it will realize that a nuclear war can but lead to the worst disaster and that in such a war there will be neither victor nor vanquished. For that reason, we are led to believe that such a war will not happen. A comparison may be made between what happened at the outset of the second world war and what is taking place today.
At the beginning of the second world war, both sides had in their possession arms which were extremely powerful, such as poison gas and bacteriological weapons. But the thought of how horrible would be gas warfare or germ warfare made both sides hesitate to use them, and in fact they were not used. Similarly, we do believe today that nuclear weapons will not be used and that the world we know and the generations to come will be protected from the awful disaster which would result from nuclear attacks.
We must recognize that mankind has known many wars, that man apparently has yet to realize the blessings of peace, and so we can suppose that there may be other wars which, even if there are no nuclear bombs dropped, will be just as dreadful and will result in a greater bloodbath than the ones we have known during the disasters of 1914-18 and 1939-45.
We know that our opponents have at their command enormous forces, powerful armies equipped with the conventional weapons we know of, that is a mighty artillery, tanks and a well trained infantry. And for that reason, it is imperative that we should have, in the face of danger, such weapons and also a well equipped army, a navy formed of most modern units and an air force with a capacity to strike or to resist any attack.
This is why it is necessary, in 1961, to deal with those defence problems, to appropriate enormous amounts in order to

be well prepared, and to remember the proverb of Juvenal, the Latin philosopher who said: Si vis pacem, para bellum.
I agree with the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Pitman) who deplored a moment ago, the fact that it is necessary today to spend large amounts to defend ourselves or to counter-attack when in fact it would be so much more preferable to use that money for more useful purposes, to improve conditions in economically weak countries and even to foster prosperity, well-being and progress in our own countries.
All sound-thinking men are of the same opinion and would like to see come to an end that arms race, those enormous war expenditures. But all sound-thinking men are also aware of the fact that a single moment of weakness on our part, such as disarmament at a time when our opponents seem to arm themselves, could very well bring us total disorder and lead us to ruin. The best proof of the truth of what I just said is that if the world was saved from the horrors of a third world war it is in fact due to the power of that organization we call NATO, which succeeded in preventing a third world war since its founding 12 years ago.
Here in Canada, regardless of political parties, we want peace. We are wishing for it, as those men of 1914-18 and of 1939-45 wished and yearned for it. But, like them, we shall fight if necessary, because, like those who fought during the last two wars, we know that our way of life is the best and that the freedom we enjoy is still man's greatest gift.
Our soldiers, in the first world war, fought with the utmost courage alongside their brothers of allied nations; it is thanks to their sacrifice that peace prevailed, and it is also thanks to what they did that we succeeded then in protecting man's freedom. Their successors, those who fought from 1939 to 1945, showed an undaunted courage on the battlefields. We owe an enormous debt to those soldiers who, at the cost of their lives and of countless sufferings, fought for freedom. We wish that our efforts to safeguard that peace for which they fought become a tribute to their gallantry and the recognition of their sacrifices.
We shall take all means at our disposal, alongside our colleagues of the other NATO countries, to preserve that peace so hardly won.

We hope that Providence will enlighten the minds of men and protect us from the disastrous consequences of a nuclear war.

Mr. Chairman, I listened with great care to the remarks which were made in committee by the hon. member for Trinity. Although I share many of the hon. member's views and believe that certain of the points which he described are worthy of consideration, I feel that other parts of his speech are not quite related to the facts, and I should like to advance certain corrections to some of the statements which he has made. The hon. gentleman did not mention today that Canada has no defence policy.
I should have. It was an omission.

That is a view that has been expressed many times by the hon. member, and he has kindly expressed it again just now. To say that Canada has no defence policy is rather silly for it is equivalent to saying that NATO has no defence policy this for the simple reason that the defence policy of Canada is based on decisions which have been taken over the years at the NATO conference table, decisions which have been arrived at only after lengthy and most careful consideration. Canada is a partner in the marvellous association of NATO which has done so much since its inception 12 years ago to preserve world peace.
Each member nation has a definite role to play in NATO, a role which has been determined according to the capabilities, abilities and resources of the individual nation. It is this role which is allotted to each nation, and which is played individually but for the interests of the collectivity which forms NATO, and which represents the strength of this organization. NATO is truly the only organization which stands between the way of life in which we believe, namely the democratic way of life, and the onslaught of the forces of communism which threaten the world today. Therefore to say that Canada has no defence policy is equivalent to saying that NATO has no defence policy, and is almost an admission that it is useless to try to defend ourselves against the forces which menace us.
We in Canada have a very definite defence policy. We have an army which plays a specific role within the NATO forces and in the shield forces of the European continent and elsewhere where our men are requested
Supply-National Defence to serve. We have a navy which plays with distinction and great efficiency a definite role in the war which is continually being waged against the danger of a submarine attack. We have an air force which plays many roles. In Europe with the F-104 plane it will act as a strike reconnaisance group in the No. 1 air division which is over there. It plays a most essential and still most necessary role of interception here in Canada against the possibility of attack by enemy manned bombers. It also plays a role in locating enemy submarines which could threaten our shores, and it trains itself continually so as to be able to destroy those submarines which may attack our country at some later date.
The defence research board plays a role of primary importance in the scientific world. Achievements of considerable importance have already been realized by the defence research board, and it is reasonable to suppose, in view of the great efforts which are being put forward by all its members, that it will carry out this useful role in the defence of our nation and the world that we know.
The hon. member for Trinity asked a few questions and made a few statements during his remarks which seemed rather strange to us. For instance, he hinted that the Americans had based their most recent defence decisions on the Liberal program which was enunciated at this rather sad performance which took place in Ottawa this last January when the Liberal party held its convention. It seems to me that the major items of policy which were contained in the speeches made by the hon. member for Trinity and others who expressed themselves at the convention were to scrap almost all the methods of defence that we have at the present time and actually almost to leave the defence of our territory to our great and powerful southern neighbours. I fail to see the resemblance between policies adopted and enunciated by the President of the United States and the other American leaders and the policies announced during that Liberal convention.
The hon. member for Trinity mentioned the fact that he was in doubt concerning the use which would be made of the 1,100 men who will be reinforcing our overseas brigade within the next few weeks. It seems to me that the answer is a very simple one. Those men will go to Germany in order to reinforce our brigade thus making it a stronger and better fighting unit, if this is still possible. I mention this last part since it is well known in Europe that the best fighting unit among the land forces in the shield force of NATO in Europe is this Canadian brigade. When I visited the SHAPE headquarters in France approximately

It was mentioned by the hon. member that this brigade is not equipped with sufficiently modern weapons. This is rather strange, because once again when I was at SHAPE over a year ago it was mentioned by one and all that the other nations of NATO were envious of the quality of training of our Canadian brigade. Where the hon. member found the figure of $10,000 per man which he mentioned I do not know.
In the blue book.

The true fact is-and he can verify this if he wishes-that the figure is much closer to between $5,000 and $6,000 per man than to the figure he mentioned. He also talked about mobile weapons, without explaining exactly what he meant by "mobile weapons". Let me tell him this, and again he can verify this if he wishes. It is a fact that our brigade in Europe, as well as the other brigade in Canada, are quite mobile and equipped with the most modern conventional equipment that can be procured under present conditions and at the present time.
Then he talks about the threat of an attack by missiles. I agree with him that such an attack would indeed be a dreadful thing if it ever occurred and there is no doubt, as we all admit, that some day the missile

threat will replace the manned bomber threat that faces us today. But there is one thing which the hon. member has not mentioned and that must be mentioned. There is at the present time and there will be for some time to come a definite threat of an attack by enemy manned bombers equipped with the most lethal weapons, and because of the presence of this threat it is considered by the NATO forces, by the NORAD command and by all sound thinking persons interested in a sound defence of this country and the northern hemisphere that we must use all possible weapons at our disposal in order to destroy the threat of these manned bombers which may still attack our shores.
Possibly the hon. member has not read what we have read, but it has been published many times in recent months that not only is the supposed enemy still flying bombers but it is still producing these bombers, and until such day as we are assured that there is no threat from a manned bomber attack we consider it our sacred duty to have suitable defences against these bombers. These suitable defences are found in the existence of the three detection lines and in the presence of the interceptor planes which we have put at the disposal of our air forces.

Perhaps you will permit me, Mr. Chairman, to thank the committee for their consideration in allowing me to continue. I was most surprised when I heard the hon. member for Trinity say that it was the government of Canada that had asked General Kuter to speak in Toronto. General Kuter did not speak in Toronto at the invitation of the Canadian government. He was invited to speak there by those in charge of the international air show. The distinguished commanding officer of NORAD made a very fine speech indeed on that occasion and I am quite sure that he did not advocate the arguments which appeared in the manifesto of the Liberal party at their recent convention. I am also quite sure that he did not share the views expressed in the house only this morning by the hon. member for Trinity.
Along with the other member nations of NATO we are trying at the present time to build up our conventional strength simply because we know that our enemy will be impressed only by the strength of our forces and by the determination which will be

shown by NATO and the forces of the member nations to defend our way of life, to defend the freedom in which we believe at all costs and in all parts of the world.
The hon. member for Trinity finally accused us of not doing enough. He said that we were not trying to build up our forces by the purchase of equipment manufactured in Canada which, by being produced in Canada, would provide employment for our people. This again is false. On the contrary, the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production are trying by all possible means to encourage our Canadian industries whenever it is possible to do so. We are doing this constantly and at all times and the best proof can be found in the production program of Bobcat vehicles, trainer aircraft, and so many other necessities.
Once again, as is the custom of members of the official opposition, the hon. member for Trinity tried to hint that there was no such thing as a defence policy for Canada. He tried to create the impression that there was only confusion in the defence department and no spirit of decision anywhere in the minds of those entrusted with the responsibility of national defence. As I said a moment ago, to say that Canada has no defence policy is to say that NATO has no defence policy since our policy is an integral part of the general NATO defence policy. To say that there is confusion and indecision in the minds of those entrusted with the care of national defence in Canada is actually casting a slur on the competence and devotion of those officers and men who are performing such a marvellous job in the service of their choice here in Canada, and elsewhere in the world.
I do not hesitate to say that we are indeed privileged to have such dedicated, competent and able men as leaders of our respective services. These men are well trained. During long careers they have given proof of their ability. The many decorations they have received and the long succession of promotions which mark their careers indicate the degree of confidence which they have enjoyed from their superiors and from the various leaders of government who have actually had in their hands the destiny of the nation during the last two or three decades. These men deserve the confidence of those who serve under them. They deserve the admiration, which they have, of those who serve with them. I do not hesitate to say that we are indeed privileged in Canada to have such distinguished leadership in all branches of our services.
If the worst should come, and if we have to fight again, I do not hesitate to say that

Mr. Chairman, the announcement of Mr. Khrushchev that the Soviet union had resumed testing of nuclear weapons is having consequences which, at the moment, can be assessed as being of far-reaching effect in dashing the hopes of mankind for a peaceful settlement of differences between the Soviet and the western powers. The explosive international situation which has taken a serious turn during recent weeks has given national defence priority over any and all other subjects for serious consideration by the government and by parliament. Indeed, the statements of the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Defense, indicate that the whole question of national defence has become one of great urgency. It is a pity, however, that the government did not foresee this urgency earlier in the year. Had we taken the necessary measures at that time to put Canada's defence effort in proper perspective, we would now be in a better position as a middle power to offer the most effective effort in the defence of peace. We believe in a permanent international police force under the United Nations. Canada should maintain, equip and train mobile forces with air and sea transport for the United Nations.
The statement of the Prime Minister on Thursday last promised new defensive measures which will increase our armed forces for overseas duty as well as speed up the program for civil defence. I, for one, will not quarrel with a frank appraisal of our present inadequate facilities for both defence and survival. All I have to do is look at the almost total absence of armoury facilities in Fort William, a city of 45,000 and serving a rural population of an additional 10,000 to be reminded of the inadequate facilities.
In about 1920 an armoury was established on the premises of an old departmental store building located on one of our busy business streets. This building served until world war II, when the city turned the Fort William hockey arena over to the federal government to provide the space required by the exigency of war, then in its third year. This building served as an armoury until 1958, at which time it was condemned and torn down. Fort William has been without an armoury ever since.
I should like to point out to the minister the highly successful army unit which was served by the old armoury. They were the 18th medium battery, Royal Canadian Artillery; the second 4th field ambulance which was to sustain the 4th field ambulance unit serving overseas. It was from the personnel of this regiment that the 35th technical squadron and a provost unit were formed. For the purpose of showing the value of an armoury at Fort William I am going to enumerate the units using that facility at the time it was closed down. They were the 118th medium battery, Royal Canadian Artillery; the 17th medical company, Royal Canadian Medical Corps; the 35th technical squadron, Royal Canadian Engineers; the provost unit, Royal


Canadian Provost Corps, the highly efficient units of sea cadets, army cadets and air force cadets.
A movement for a new armoury was initiated immediately after the building was condemned by the fire marshal for the province of Ontario. In 1956 the prairie command gave top priority to this building, and I am informed it was near the top of the list in the Department of National Defence. The significant reason this request failed to materialize was the abandonment of the 67th as a regiment. However, in 1959 a petition for a new armoury at Fort William was signed by 5,000 responsible property owners of the city, supported by the Fort William city council, the chamber of commerce and the Canadian Legion unit of the area, and it was presented to the then minister of national defence. The city of Fort William made an offer, which still stands, of a suitable site free of charge. This site was approved by the prairie command which had jurisdiction of the area at that time.
At this point, Mr. Chairman, I wish to stress a few irrefutable reasons why the establishment of an armoury in Fort William should not be delayed. Fort William is the granary of the continent and merits special consideration for army protection as it is vulnerable to attack from many directions. Fort William has always had a strong military organization and the nucleus is available for a renewed effort to recruit a new unit.
Decentralization of military and emergency measures organization forces is considered essential. Fort William is located in the centre of Canada, ideally located for a training and operational base.
The cadet movement is particularly strong, but requires a proper armoury in which to train our youth. Recruiting is slow, for the absence of a central location and adequate equipment discourages not only the officers but also the potential cadet.
Fort William is interested in organizing a mobile unit as part of the emergency measures organization. This is required to support our survival plans, and will do much to encourage our citizens to take an active part in protective planning.
The debate on the issue of national defence has amply demonstrated that at present the Canadian armed forces lack strength and equipment for any effort Canada may be asked to perform on behalf of the United Nations in the interest of peace. Whether we like it or not, and ruling out the probability of a nuclear war which to sane people everywhere is unthinkable, we are faced with a prolonged chilling cold war, and it is the duty of this parliament to see

that our conventional forces are built up to full strength. We need men and equipment, and the facilities to train our manpower.
There are in our midst some well inten-tioned men and women who believe that we should not spend money on armaments, and that our tax dollar would be better spent in building schools and hospitals. The uncomfortable facts, however, are that we cannot indulge in the luxury of neutrality. This has been tried before by some European nations, and to their sorrow. Who would believe for one minute that, if the Soviet union were involved in an all out war with the United States, Russia would respect our neutrality?
Those who advocate a neutral position for Canada are simply trying to avoid unpleasant facts in the hope that they will vanish in the wake of wishful thinking. At the same time, it would be a mistake to believe that a strong Canada should have nuclear weapons for its own defence and the defence of the alliance. These weapons should be left in the hands of those now in possession of them.
Notwithstanding the belief expressed by some members-and some people believe it- that the old weapons would be obsolete and no good in a future war, that money spent on conventional arms is money wasted, that only nuclear weapons would be used and that as a result humanity would be wiped off the face of the earth, I should like to remind those people that in world war II poison gas was not used by either side. In spite of the fact that both sides possessed enormous supplies of poison gas capable of exterminating whole armies, gas was not used. Why?
It was not used because both sides knew the terrible consequences of poisoning whole populations. I therefore believe that in the event of a clash over Berlin the knowledge of total annihilation will prevent the touching off of a nuclear war.
Canada's contribution and influence as a member of NATO can best serve by playing a role fitted to her capability such as that of having Canadian troops employed as part of any United Nations emergency force anywhere in the world. I was very much pleased to hear the Associate Minister of National Defence say that the Bobcat program will be implemented. I understand that the Canada Car plant at Fort William will have an opportunity to share in its production. I hope that situation will come about. In any event it is a vehicle which we should have not only for our own use but for that of our allies, and some of the underdeveloped coun-90205-6-520J

However, with all the sincerity at my command I suggest that we should not fall into the temptation of confining the building-up to a much too small and poorly equipped force. Unfortunately, having listened to the speeches from the other side of the house, I find myself a little bit at a loss. In the last year they have been in and out of NATO like a drunk in a revolving door; and from what was said today, it is a little bit difficult to gather, whether actually as of September 12 they are in favour of Canada's participation in NATO or not. We heard the hon. member for Kootenay West the other day quoting the resolution of his party as adopted at their convention and which seemed to give lip service to participation in NATO but said that Canada alone, one of 15 nations, should change the whole purpose and direction of that organization. This, of course, is one of the penalties of alliances, that no one nation can control completely the direction and the policies of the organization. But I think it is fair to say that Canada has had and will continue to have a very large influence on the policies of NATO. Those influences have been constructive and have worked toward a strengthening of the organization and an increasing of its effectiveness.

speechtext:
I imagine the minister left that sentence out of his speech simply because he felt it had been said so often and had been made so obvious as to become a cliche. Obviously our defence policy flows from our general national policy toward the world situation and toward other nations in the world.
The minister said-and I should like to repeat it because I think it is most important- that our objectives are two in number. Many people these days who discuss defence start somewhere away on down the line in methods, but you cannot develop any effective policy in any line unless you first consider what you are trying to do. Therefore I should like to emphasize the two parts that sum up our objective-prevention of war and the maintenance of freedom. If you try only to consider the first you will get a policy very different from the one you get if you realize the necessity of maintaining both objectives.
It has also been said that the major instrument of our policy is NATO. It seems to me that one of the things that cannot be emphasized too much, although in the last few days it has been said frequently in this house, is that the great virtue of NATO is that it works. Let me recall to the minds of those who question the efficacy of NATO what the situation was in Europe before that organization was formed.
Hon. members will recall that Czechoslovakia had recently fallen to the communists. It will be recalled that the communist forces in some of the western European countries were so strong as to give great cause for concern. One did not know from day to day what might happen in Italy, and even in France we were uncertain. One can date from the formation of the NATO alliance the halt of the communist advance westward across Europe. One can also date from the formation of this alliance the rehabilitation of the countries of western Europe. This involvement by the United States, Britain and Canada in the affairs of Europe gave to those countries and to the people of those countries the courage, confidence and realization that they were not alone in their troubles that allowed them to rebuild after the ravages of the second world war.
Anyone who stands up in Canada today and says we should abandon NATO, in almost any circumstances, has an obligation to bear in mind the accomplishments of NATO and has an obligation also to recommend some other arrangement which would give us and our friends and allies the degree of security that has been provided by that organization.
There are those who say we should abandon NATO, NORAD and our other defence alliances because then our prestige at the United
[Mr. Hellyer.l
Nations, our prestige among the neutral countries of the world, would grow. In other words they advocate a defence by moral suasion.
Let those who consider that to be a responsible policy for the Dominion of Canada think of how much effect moral suasion had on Mr. Khrushchev when he ordered the resumption of nuclear testing. How much influence has the moral suasion of the Belgrade group and the pleas of Mr. Nehru, who personally went to Moscow? How much influence has that had on the continuation of these tests which, as we have heard this morning, may have the most disastrous effects if carried on long enough.
It seems to me that when we consider a policy to protect ourselves against the depredations of communism in the world we must rely on something more concrete than moral suasion. In fact we must rely on creating a situation in the world wherein they will not dare to start a war.
We know from the writings of their leaders and from the speeches of Mr. Khrushchev and his predecessors that it is a belief held by the communists that they have a historical right to take over world society. We know also, because this too they have told us, that they believe the end justifies the means, that they are justified in achieving their ends by any means, military, economic, subversive or whatever.
Our first duty in the west, then, is to create a situation wherein they cannot achieve these ends by military means. This is the strategy of the alliances to which we belong particularly that of NATO. Once again let me point out that the great virtue of this strategy is that it works.
I should like now to pass for a moment to the question of air defence. The hon. member for Trinity last year and again this year put forward the view that there is no necessity for a defence against manned bombers because manned bombers are obsolete. The hon. member may be correct, but I *wonder whether the gentlemen in the Kremlin have heard about, it.
Would you give the source, please?
