I have not the page here. I got it last year and I can get it again from the speech of the hon. member this morning. We also know from the press, from the accounts of the Moscow air show not long ago, that there did not seem to be much evidence in that display of sabre rattling that the Russians had abandoned manned aircraft. In fact, of course there is a change from manned aircraft to missiles, but what so many people, including my hon. friend from Trinity, seem to forget or overlook is that

these changes do not take place overnight. They cannot take place overnight. Because some missiles exist which might be used in any attack upon North America, and very probably would be used in any attack upon North America, this does not mean that should such an attack come-or should such an attack be considered, which is perhaps the better way of putting it-it would be necessary at the present time, to the best of our information, for the Russians to plan on using a considerable number of manned bombers.
Thus if we can create a defensive situation on the North American continent where they can have no confidence that a sufficient number of their bombers would get through to accomplish their mission, they can take no rational decision to attack. No doubt there will come a day when the threat of the manned bomber can be ignored. Figuring out the intentions or possible plans of a potential enemy is not an exact science but to say that because there are missiles we should abandon defence against the manned bomber is tantamount to saying that because there are high explosive artillery shells we should abandon the steel helmet. We have to try on this continent as in our global strategy to create a situation whereby it will be impossible for our potential enemy to take a position to attack. The defence of the deterrent against manned bombers is part of the arrangement to do that.
There has been a great deal said on the question of mobility and particularly the mobility of the 4th Canadian infantry brigade group in Germany. I think it should be emphasized that this brigade is completely mobile. That is to say it has within its own resources the capacity to move itself. I remember that some time ago I was visiting the brigade. I had to leave one morning at about 7.30. Various arrangements were made to get me to an airport. When I got up at about 6.30 I found that three quarters of an hour before a surprise exercise had been sprung on the brigade by higher command and they had been ordered to move. Within three quarters of an hour the brigade which had been sleeping and which had no warning, had completely disappeared from the area. All the men had embarked in their vehicles and had moved off in tactical formation. To me this indicates a very high degree of mobility indeed.
We are told we must have forces ready to serve the United Nations. I believe the hon. member for Fort William said we did not have any such forces. This, of course, is utter nonsense. On each occasion when we have been called upon by the United Nations Canada has produced the forces that were requested. In fact, all of Canada's forces,
Supply-National Defence particularly her army, are in a practically constant state of readiness for the United Nations. Their equipment and vehicles are ideally suited to participation in any emergency that might arise. As I said this has been demonstrated both in the Gaza strip and the Congo. The forces being used so effectively there are not equipped differently from the rest of Canada's armed forces. As hon. members well know we have increased our capacity to transport our forces by air to any part of the world. It should be borne in mind that these United Nations tasks do not usually require heavy weapons. It is almost inconceivable that a situation would arise in which the United Nations would call for a force to make an assault landing or an airborne attack on some area in the world. Therefore I think it can be truly said that with respect to the type of forces that the United Nations are liable to call for, Canada is ideally equipped to supply them when the time comes.
It seems to me that one of the reasons people in this country occasionally advocate such impractical ideas in relation to our defence is that the consequences of a failure are so much greater today than they have been in the past. If one of our twin objectives, as I mentioned earlier, is to prevent war, the failure to achieve this objective would lead to the most terrible consequences, but this being so, it is no answer to the dilemma to say that like the ostrich we should therefore put our heads in the sand and say we will have nothing to do with it.
I believe it was the hon. member for Peterborough who said that a conflict between the United States and the U.S.S.R. would have no effect on us at all. I would say to the hon. gentleman we would certainly be affected and must therefore do all in our power to prevent it. Surely the way to do that is to do what Canada has always done, to live up to her international obligations and maintain the reputation she has built because she has lived up to her international obligations. We must not throw up our hands in despair and say that this problem is too big for us, that we will leave it to the big boys, that we will leave it to the United States or to the United States and the Soviet union and that we will concentrate on foreign aid. Foreign aid is a good and necessary measure and in my view it is part of our defence, in a manner of speaking, in that economic and ideological war that goes on under what might be called the umbrella of the nuclear threat. But the first obligation of the government of Canada in the area of defence is to do everything in its power for the security of the people of Canada. This we have done and this we will continue to do to the best of the ability of this country.

Supply-National Defence
As the minister said, we have recently decided on an increase in our contribution to NATO in the form of additional men for both the air division and the brigade in Germany. These in themselves will be valuable additions to the forces in western Europe; but more than that, it seems to me, they are a restatement of our faith in that organization and our realization of the necessity for it. Once again we have said to our allies: we stand with you in the defence of freedom and here is the earnest of our pledge. It is a cliche, if you wish, but never has it been more true than today that we will stand together or separately we will fall.

Mr. Chairman:
In my judgement, a Liberal is a man who ought to stand as a restraining force against an extravagant policy. He is a man who ought to keep cool in the presence of Jingo clamour. He is a man who believes that the confidence between nations begets confidence, and that the spirit of peace and good will makes the safety it seeks. And, above all, I think a Liberal is a man who should keep a sour look for scaremongers of every kind and of every size, however distinguished, however ridiculous-and sometimes the most distinguished are the most ridiculous-
These are not my words, sir; these are the words of Winston Churchill. It is not enough that we always speak and think in defence matters in terms of contention. It surely is necessary that we have something in the nature of a goal and a purpose. What is somewhat disturbing to people on this side of the house is the fact that when the Minister of National Defence is in the house the Secretary of State for External Affairs is not, and when the Secretary of State for External Affairs is in the house it appears that the Minister of National Defence is not.
You will forgive us, sir, if in thinking in terms of defence-
Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member does not want to be incorrect or unfair. I should like to point out to him that X was here practically throughout the entire debate on external affairs.
Facts never bother the Liberals.
What about the other half of the remark?
The Secretary of State for External Affairs is busy today with Dr. Stikker and this afternoon the president of Iceland is coming in.

I accept the fact that I must have been in error. I did notice on a couple of occasions that when the Secretary of State for External Affairs was speaking the Minister of National Defence was not present. I withdraw the observation of course but

I made it for another reason. It appeared very clear to us that the policies expounded so clearly by the Secretary of State for External Affairs did not appear to be in harmony with many points in the policies expounded by the Minister of National Defence. May I say this. We have heard something in the last few days.
May I ask the hon. member a question.
At the end of my speech I will be happy to answer any questions.

The
hon. member for Leeds has the floor. If he wishes to yield to the hon. member asking the question he may or may not do so. I believe he has indicated he does not wish the hon. gentleman to question him at this point in his speech.

May I say that today we have had words which seem to substantiate the fact that what we have is defence policy by proxy. It appears that the policy is always formulated in NATO headquarters or in some other headquarters. What we are interested in is that there be something in the nature of Canadian policy with respect to national defence.
I think I made myself rather clear in the external affairs debate when I asserted the need for a strengthened military machine armed with conventional weapons and ready to meet challenge wherever it comes in the free world. Freedom is threatened but there are other factors that have to be considered. I should like to quote a few words from an article on foreign affairs by Sir Anthony Eden called "The Slender Margin of Safety". He said:
Since 1940 the Western European powers have voluntarily agreed to the independence of 18 different countries with a population of more than 600 million people. During the same period the communist countries have brought under their rule 12 previously free countries with a population of more than 120 million.
One of the things we have to consider at this time is the nature of the type of leadership which Canada may very reasonably be expected to provide for those people who have been brought into freedom. This by no means must be by virtue of what is so contemptuously referred in this house on different occasions as neutralism. May I quote from the memoirs of Mr. Truman who said:
We laboured to construct a weapon of such overpowering force that the enemy could be forced to yield swiftly once we could resort to it.
This remains the thinking of the speakers on the government's side, as has been demonstrated in this debate. I continue with the quotation:

They recommended further that it should be used without specific warning and against a target that would clearly show its devastating strength.
And so on. I continue:
Four cities were finally recommended as targets: Hiroshima, Kokura, Niigata, and Nagasaki.
Then, he heard about the bomb being dropped and he said:
I was greatly moved. I telephoned Byrnes aboard ship to give him the news and then said to the group of sailors around me, "This is the greatest thing in history. It's time for us to get home."
We read the news item which appeared in the Ottawa Journal which came out a few minutes ago and which referred to the extent of nuclear fall-out.
I should now like to quote a few words in French from Montesquieu:
(Translation):
If I knew something was helpful to my country and prejudicial to Europe or helpful to Europe and prejudicial to the human race, I would consider it a crime.
(Text):
A man who now enjoys the position of United States ambassador to the United Nations namely Adlai Stevenson said:
There are those who say that disarmament is impossible until political settlements have been reached and confidence restored. I disagree. I believe the nuclear arms race with weapons of mass destruction is a new element and in itself a cause of tension. Fear will not vanish until the arms race is arrested.
I think it is rather important that some matters of great moment, matters of national defence be discussed at this time. May I refer to the information which was gathered together for the special committee on defence expenditures in 1960. It was produced by the then minister of national defence, General Pearkes. This is what he said:
No one nation can afford a unilateral defence. Canada's defence effort must not be viewed in isolation but rather as a contribution to the combined deterrent of the western alliance. Our defence expenditures are not providing complete protection but in combination with others, they are contributing to the over-all effectiveness of an insurance against possible aggression.
With this I think we all agree. However, I think it has got to be more than that. NATO is composed of many different nations of many different backgrounds and of many different possibilities of service. I should now like to refer to an article which appears in the bulletin of the atomic scientists. It is called "The Future of Western Deterrent Power", by Alastair Buchan, and was published in 1960. He speaks about the considerations inherent in being a non-nuclear alliance member, and says:
The first step would involve a negotiation, possibly prolonged and difficult, to determine the considerations which should govern the siting of the land and water-based Polaris or other solid-fueled
Supply-National Defence missiles which will replace the existing bombers. Should they be sited in Germany? Almost certainly not for sound political reasons affecting relationships within the alliance and with Moscow which most intelligent Germans accept. Should Norway be asked to reconsider the refusal to accept nuclear bases since her terrain is ideally suited to their dispersal and hardening? Again probably not for equally sound reasons concerned with the delicacy of the political balance in Scandinavia. Should they be sited in Britain? Yes. In Benelux? Probably. In France? Yes.
This is the opinion of Alastair Buchan whom many of us knew rather well. He recognizes that in NATO there will be different functions and purposes. I remind this committee that only one nation with the background and the potential for the development of the atomic bomb refused as a matter of principle to do so, and that country was Canada. The fact that we live in close proximity to the very powerful and beloved neighbour to the south enables us to speak frankly to this great nation. We are able to furnish military equipment and personnel of absolutely the best type and quality possible, men who are prepared to take their stand in danger spots but without nuclear arms. We recognize that behind the NATO shields there may be nuclear support, but our troops should be men of courage with manifestly no offensive purposes at all. The principle behind them is to defend the peace. This is the most important cause to which we can contribute.
We should like to see in Canada something in the nature of a clear, enunciated, articulated policy. There is some suggestion that we are not in favour of NATO. This suggestion is ridiculous. After all, we remember the occasion when the University of London granted an LL.D. degree to the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. The citation referred to him as the chief architect of NATO. We are proud of NATO. Our fear is that NATO may get off the rails. We must have confidence in NATO. Then we will be able to say, "We will march wherever you lead." There are powerful forces in NATO and there are weaker forces in NATO, and we have got to be in the position of being what Toynbee has referred to as a dominant minority in NATO, a creative minority, a minority that is prepared to try to have an effect and influence on the lives of the people of the world at large. I believe this is the only way that this dreadful holocaust can be avoided.
With respect to NORAD, I should like to refer to a book which in some circles is not popular. However, I believe we must read it and read it very carefully because the man who write it is a well informed, knowledgeable and respected member of the press. I am referring to the book, "Peacemaker or Powder-monkey", written by James M. Minifie. He has this to say:

Supply-National Defence
NORAD had been mentioned at cabinet level during the last months of the dying Liberal government of Louis St. Laurent. But it had not reached the stage of cabinet decision. Although Mr. Pearkes appeared to have been under the impression that the preceding cabinet had agreed on NORAD, this was almost certainly not the case. It was the child of the new Conservative government-as unlikely an offspring as could have been wished upon an administration which had made a fetish of Canadian independence and had run a spectacularly effective election campaign, not indeed on anti-Americanism, but on a pro-Canadian nationalism which NORAD made nonsense of... a nation which has put part of its forces under foreign command in a two-way deal with a vastly more powerful neighbour has lost its independence. Canada has become a military satellite of the United States sun. The hard-won power to decide on peace or war has passed from Ottawa via Washington ...
I submit that we do not yet know the extent to which we are in fact a satellite of the United States in this important regard. There have been hints and suggestions that there are at the present time nuclear armed aircraft under United States command which are patrolling Canadian skies. We do not know the facts. We are left in ignorance and I am sure the Canadian people at the present time are quite ignorant of what is happening. I say, sir, with all respect to some people on the other side whom I regard as close friends, that this is typically Conservative in its approach. It represents the attitude which says that we should not decide for ourselves.
If any hon. members would care to do so they can go to the parliamentary library and look at the debates that occurred in the year 1910 on the naval bill. You will remember how cries of treason rang through the chamber when Laurier said that we should have a navy of our own, that we should build it, that we should produce a flotilla and should decide what we were going to build although it would, of course, fit in with the British picture. There were Conservative members in the house in those days who rose and said, "No, definitely not". Their position was that it was improper for Canada to do this, that we should simply ask England what amount of money they wanted and then give it to them and let them spend it. I think that is not the typical view of Canadians generally.
If you want to take another illustration of the same thing, there is the argument relating to military command. Can we in Canada decide to govern our own forces? In the Chanak incident of 1923 Mackenzie King said Canada would not necessarily go to war on that matter over Turkey and in the result he perhaps saved Britain from serious and disastrous consequences. If my friend on my left will contain himself for a minute, I should like to refer to a little book which has been cited all over the world. It is entitled, "Democracy in World Politics". It is very elementary, particularly so in the light of all

the gadgetry and hardware that have been the subject of discussion today. The author has this to say:
If violence breaks out, the play of this principle helps to limit the breakdown to the minimum needed to defeat aggression and, above all, to restore the peace. If a nation uses force in aggression against its neighbour, that neighbour and its allies, and indeed the entire free community, acting through and within the principles of the United Nations charter, may justifiably use-in fact have an obligation to use-collective force to repel that aggression. This does not, however, give them a moral licence to attempt, by the use of overwhelming and unlimited force, to destroy completely the aggressor society.
This is developed to some extent in this book. There is a very simple proposition put forward with which all of us who have anything to do with the police courts are familiar. The law discussed is the law of assault and the author says:
The doctrine that only a limited use of force, proportionate to the circumstances and strictly necessary to accomplish specific objectives, can be justified as self-defence is, I think, inherent in the principles of natural law. Certainly it is basic to the domestic law of all civilized peoples.
Then he refers to the judgement of Mr. Justice Martin of the Saskatchewan court of appeal in the case of MacNeill and Hill and quotes these words:
While the law recognizes the right of selfdefence, the right to repel force with force, no right is to be abused and the right of self-defence is one which may easily be abused. The force employed must not be out of proportion to the apparent urgency of the occasion.
Then he quotes the Canadian Criminal Code, section 66:
Everyone authorized by law to use force is criminally responsible for any excess according to the nature and quality of the act which constitutes the excess.
Then he goes on to refer to the case of State v. Cephus, a well-known American authority, and follows that with our English authority, Halsbury's Laws of England. He then refers to the Encyclopedic Dalloz which expresses the French law to the same effect. Then he comes to the conclusion to which I have referred, that if violence breaks out the principle of limited force limits the breakdown to the minimum needed to defeat aggression.
You would need a big police force.
I would be glad to answer questions-
It is not a question; it is an observation.

With respect to the observation about a police force, may I refer to something that may appear strange in a defence debate. Perhaps one person who never

intended to exert great influence on the commonwealth but nevertheless did so more than anyone else in the world was Mahatma Gandhi, and I should like to read a few brief lines respecting him:
Naked little Hindu fakir,
Vexing to the powers that be,-
Praying, spinning, scheming, fasting,
How absurd to such as we.
We never understood his wisdom,
Suddenly the tragic end.
Pistol shots that stirred the nations.
All mankind had lost a friend.
Stripes to him and to his children.
Weary years in British quod.
Dusty miles to briny ocean.
Raised on earth a child of God.
Fractious world beset with sorrows, Searching for what's brave and true,
Hover closer, gentle Bapu We need aid from such as you.
I think the situation right now is such that we in the western world need something of the personality of Gandhi. We cannot apply Gandhi's method to the particular situation confronting us. Any person who suggested such a thing would be foolish, but would it really be foolish to think of Canada taking these principles that are bold and brave and acting on them with our conventional weapons as and when the need arises and protected by the shield of NATO and our NATO allies? In a situation such as Berlin today we have a battalion, such as that of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, the Black Watch with their pipes, or there are the R.C.R.'s whom I saw performing tremendously at Fort Henry a few days ago. Is this the type of thing that might appeal to the imagination of the world? We Canadians have taken on a great many assignments. We have in this house right now people who participated at Ypres and at the Somme and at so many other places. There was the Dieppe raid. Some of these things were foolish ventures. I think it is not at all unreasonable to say that in our Canadian army today we have men of idealism and courage who are prepared to assume the risk inherent in conventional weaponry. But we are not getting frank answers on this score. We are getting the old answer that the soldiers must have the best equipment possible.
I put it to the house that this is no answer and that we have not frightened Russia at all. Maybe Mr. Truman was able to frighten Japan a few years ago but the Russians are in a different position. There is only one thing greater than nuclear force and if I may refer to a speech made at the University of Oslo by the author of the book to which I have referred, Mr. Pearson said in that speech that ideas can also be explosive. I think this is something that we have got to bear in mind.
90205-6-521
Supply-National Defence
The person who wrote this book on the principles of defence was not absolutely naive and ignorant about war. He participated in the first great commando effort in the world, the Gallipoli campaign in 1915. It involved something like 120,000 British troops and there were 50,000 dead when it finally failed. The force was made up of British, Australians, New Zealanders, Gurkhas and many others and he brings to this subject the experience he had in those days and the war years that followed. He will recall that in those days, all troops did not do the same thing, just as all troops did not do the same thing for the British eighth army. You could not feed them the same way, you could not arm them the same way. They had different roles. My friend the hon. member for Edmonton West will recall that the Gurkhas would do things at night that his loyal Edmonton regiment troops would not do. They had special skills. In the role that I have suggested our Canadian militia could serve magnificently. We have a good record, a record of not being a dirty army. We have always had this reputation and that is a role we have to preserve.
Now, referring to the particular problem before us, there is an important article written by Pierre M. Gallois entitled, "New Teeth for NATO". In this article he recognizes the four stages in depth in which NATO defence can be developed. Conventional weapons at the front, a second nuclear shield until at last we finally go across the seas with the possibility of intervention by strategic air command. We suggest that we take the courageous role of world peacemaker and be on the spot, be there with the weapons we can carry, such as light artillery and things that are mobile.
In the publication the Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science, there is an article by Senator Saltonstall entitled, "Western Military Strength and Security." In this article, he says:
There are two permanent issues concerning the defence posture which have a particularly important relationship to the philosophy of deterrence. These are: (a) the strengthening of weapons and equipment suitable to fight in situations of limited conflict, and (b) the efforts to bring about dependable agreements on weapons tests, arms control, and eventual disarmament.
I quote from the article at another point:
Secretary McNamara commented there had been a tendency since the end of the Korean war to emphasize the nuclear capabilities of limited war forces. Although such use is essential, the Pentagon is careful to point out, the non-nuclear capability of conventional forces is stressed in the current plan in order to provide greater versatility.

Mr. Chairman, while I rise to take part in this debate, I do not pretend to be an expert on international politics or in the field of military or civil defence, but I want to express the concern that Canadians have felt in their hearts and minds because of recent developments, and more particularly because of the Russians' decision to resume nuclear tests.
I was astounded by the fact that for more than a year-and we have the evidence today-while negotiations were going on in Geneva about a final nuclear test ban, when western and other free countries represented at those conferences were discussing with sincerity and honesty, Russia was not of the same mind because, according to experts, it takes months to prepare an atomic blast.
Only a few days ago, Mr. Khrushchev made a threat which he accompanied by an imperative gesture as usual, and since then, the Russians have exploded six atomic bombs. Thus, while discussions were still going on in Geneva, while sincere and free countries were working together to put a stop to those nuclear tests, the Russians were secretly and dishonestly intending to resume them, and they have just proved it by exploding six atomic bombs.
Mr. Chairman, the Canadian people are greatly concerned, of course, and we are presently going through dark days, not only because of the material consequences of those explosions, but also of the distrust that is spreading among nations.
That spirit of distrust, a venerable old man has painted it out very well in his recent encyclical letter Mater et Magistra. I should like to quote a short passage of John XXIII's encyclical:
90205-6-521J
Supply-National Defence
It can thus be understood how individuals and nations are getting more and more convinced of the urgent necessity of understanding and co-operation. However, it seems that men. especially those who shoulder the heaviest responsibilities, are incapable of causing the one and the other. The reason for that incapacity lies not in science, technology or economics, but in the lack of mutual trust.
A little further, John XXIII states:
The lack of mutual trust is due to the fact that the activities of men, especially those who bear the heaviest responsibilities, are inspired by different or radically opposed concepts of life. Unfortunately, some of these concepts do not take into account the existence of a moral order, of an order which is transcendent, universal, not absolute and of equal value for all. It becomes therefore impossible to meet and to fully agree, with all security, in the light of a same law of justice accepted and followed by all. It is true that the word "justice" and the phrase "the requirements of justice" continue to be used by everyone; but that word and that phrase have for each one a different or contrary meaning.
Indeed, there are between the Soviet bloc and the alliance of western free countries two basic differences in their concept of life. While we in the free nations, the Christian nations, the western nations, are trying to establish peace for the triumph of spiritual values and the installation of the rule of God over His creatures, our opponents are looking for peace-at least they say so-but only through a search for material and materialistic aims, without any belief in the spiritual values, without any belief in the dignity of the human being.
That is the real trouble in our hearts, and it is in such a climate of distrust, which becomes increasingly troubling, that we have all these important discussions in international organizations.
It must be said to the credit of Canada and of the present administration that they wish to pursue and promote negotiations in order to lessen that distrust. Furthermore, this government is to be credited-and this needs to be said-in the face of communist ideas spreading across the world, for embodying in its legislation that fundamental assurance and very concrete expression of human rights and freedoms. We cannot repeat it too often: those rights and freedoms are, initially and in final analysis, of God's creation.
That is the fine example the government has given the whole world by its bill of rights. In the pursuit of its activities, it recognizes man's dignity, the Canadian citizen's dignity, that of any citizen of the world, and it is yearning for peace in order to ensure the triumph of spiritual values and the recognition of God's rule over His creatures.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like to say at the outset that I intend to be very brief as I am sure there are many hon. members who would like to take part in the debate on this very interesting subject.
I think this is the third occasion upon which this bill has been introduced by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). I am happy to say that I feel he has been sincere on each occasion in introducing the bill. However, I must admit that he has failed to convince me of the necessity for this bill at this particular time.
The hon. member proposes to ask for an amendment to section 3 of the Canada Fair
Private Bills
Employment Practices Act whereby the act binds Her Majesty in right of Canada and servants and agents of Her Majesty.
I think it would be wise for us very briefly to review what the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act provides. In short, it provides that no employer shall discriminate in so far as the employment of employees or the terms or conditions of employment are concerned because of race, national origin, colour or religion. It also applies, of course, to hiring agencies and to trade unions, whereby it states that trade unions shall not discriminate against its members or prevent potential members from becoming members of the union.
This bill is a very short one. It merely seeks to make the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act apply to the crown and crown agencies. However, I would remind the hon. gentleman that crown corporations are already taken care of and must apply this act in all their dealings with employees. At the present time crown corporations come within the ambit of the act.
Section 3 of the act reads as follows:
This act applies to and in respect of employment upon or in connection with any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, including, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing, (m) the employment by any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the government of Canada of employees.
This bill would make the act apply to employees of of Her Majesty in the right of Canada. We may thus eliminate crown corporations because they have to abide by the act as it now stands. I firmly believe that the federal government is living up to the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act all along the line. I know it is the duty of the unemployment insurance commission not to practice discrimination on any grounds of race, national origin, colour or religion. I also realize that the Department of Public Works has inserted in its contracts a clause that takes care of this matter. A similar clause is inserted in all supply contracts that are entered into by the government. I am therefore convinced that the Canadian government is fulfilling its duty in applying in all its departments the principles of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. The province of Ontario has a similar act and I feel that other provinces are doing an excellent job in promoting fair employment practices.
I am proud to say that I come from a municipality where no discrimination is exercised in the hiring of employees. I therefore feel that the bill as introduced by the hon. member for Skeena is unnecessary at the present time.

Private Bills
If the hon. gentleman will pause to reflect he will realize that a special committee was set up to study the Civil Service Act. During the meetings of that committee this very question was considered by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell). As reported at page 521 of the minutes and proceedings of the committee dated June 20, 1961, the hon. member for Carleton had this to say:

May X ask the leave of the committee to revert to clause 33. The members of the committee will remember at the meeting of Friday, April 21, that there was presented to us a letter from the Canadian Jewish Congress in which they asked that there be inserted in the Civil Service Act a non-discrimination clause. That matter has had some consideration especially as to where, if such a clause were to be placed in the act, it should be placed. The advice of the draftsman is that if such a clause is to be inserted that it be inserted in clause 33.
The committee accepted an amendment in these words:
The commission may in relation to any position or any class or grade prescribe qualifications as to age, residence or any other matters that in the opinion of the commission are necessary or desirable having regard to the nature of the duties to be performed, but in so doing the commission shall not discriminate against any person by reason of race, national origin, colour or religion.
This amendment has been inserted in clause 33. The committee has reported to the house. If this is passed by parliament the very thing the hon. member for Skeena seeks to accomplish in introducing Bill No. C-9 will be attained. Since the introduction of his bill the bill of rights has been passed by parliament. The bill of rights will also accomplish what the hon. member for Skeena wishes to see brought about by the amendment as outlined in Bill No. C-9.
I believe I have covered most of the main points on the bill before us. I agreed with the general principle of the bill in that it calls upon the government of Canada to introduce provisions relating to the abolition of discrimination which I am sure we all wish to see eliminated in our land. I believe that the government should be bound by all the laws it applies to its citizens. I feel that the purpose of Bill No. C-9 will be well taken care of when the amendment to clause 33 of Bill No. C-71 relating to the Civil Service Act is adopted and passed by parliament.
I am unable to support this bill at this time for the following reasons. First, the hon. member who introduced the bill failed to give sufficient cases in which the government is not living up to the provisions of the Canada Fail Employment Practices Act. Second, I feel that the federal government is now providing equality of opportunity without discrimination

on the basis of race, national origin, colour or religion. Third, I feel that the provisions of Bill No. C-9 will be well taken care of when the amended Civil Service Act is passed. Fourth, I feel that what the hon. member seeks to accomplish by this bill has already been accomplished by the introduction of the bill of rights.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say I am in complete agreement with many of the remarks made by the previous speaker. I think that all Canadians, whether we are referring to private employment practices or employment practices in relation to the government or crown, have no patience with and absolutely abhor anything which smacks of discrimination. I appreciate that we can speak only of our own particular areas. Whether with respect to government employment matters or employment practices in private enterprise, I am proud to be able to say that I have never seen anything in the nature of discrimination in the area I represent. I know of no incident of this kind in the past either in relation to government or private enterprise hiring.
I do not say this in a holier than thou attitude and I do not say this in comparing ourselves with other nations, but I feel that Canadians in general-although there are some notable exceptions-can be very proud of their history. I repeat that with some notable exceptions Canadians are able to look with great pride at their past in this regard. Canadians in general do not tolerate discrimination on the basis of race, national origin, colour or religion. We see this in the field of education and in many other areas.
The Canada Fair Employment Practices Act came into effect on July 1, 1953. As has been pointed out, in general outline the act states that no employer can discriminate with respect to colour, race, national origin or religion. The general terms of the act also prevent an employer from using a hiring agency to obtain the same end. The general provisions of the act relating to trade unions state that no trade union may bar an individual from membership on grounds of discrimination. The act does not allow a trade union to expel a member or employee on grounds of discrimination.
It has been said that the bill before the house asks that its provisions be made applicable to the crown. I can only say I agree with the previous speaker. The sponsor of the bill before us this afternoon seeks to attain an end. Nobody within or without this house can quarrel with that end. In all sincerity, I say that what we are discussing is the means

to attain that end. We are all against discrimination. All Canadians are against it no matter how or where it exists.
I was interested to read that in speaking for his party the sponsor of this legislation said that so often the sanction for many laws was a state of mind. Perhaps he meant that so many of our laws come into being by custom and by tradition. I find it a little strange that a member representing the socialist party and speaking about socialist doctrine should advance such a theory. I have always thought that the socialists feel you can legislate for a state of mind.

speechtext: This shows how mistaken you are.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE
speechtext:
I make this reference only in passing. I underline the fact that I feel the end result of this legislation can be best attained by a revision of the Civil Service Act itself.
Again I say that nobody wants discrimination. It has been pointed out time and time again that in relation to civil service hiring practices there has never been a case of discrimination. If anybody inside or outside this house has any doubt in his mind in this regard he should bring it immediately to the attention of the government. I repeat that there has never been discrimination in relation to race, colour, religion or national origin with respect to government hiring of personnel. Therefore I ask this very simple question. Why in essence is the bill so described before the house this afternoon? I do not doubt its sincerity. Yet, when one realizes that there has never been any discrimination one wonders why this particular bill is before us. We agree that it is seeking a very desirable end.
It is admitted that in 1942 there was a question about colour in a civil service questionnaire. I am not quite sure of the kind of questionnaire it was. I am not going to admit, state or even imply for a minute that discrimination was involved but since that date the question has been dropped.
The civil service commission today, as in the past, is following a policy of non-discrimination. This goes without saying. If there is more than a modicum of doubt in anybody's mind perhaps it is only right that we should be discussing this most important matter in the Canadian House of Commons. I repeat what I said. If there has ever been a case of discrimination in relation to government, then it is the duty of the citizen or the member who has knowledge of it to bring it to the attention of the government.
Private Bills
To our knowledge discrimination has never been knowingly practised. There has never been such a case.
If Bill No. C-9 is to be passed it occurs to me that the penalty section of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act would likewise need amendment. If we should pass this act today we would inevitably see that many anomalies would arise.
I have pointed out the fact that a revision of the Civil Service Act itself would be the best way to attain the ends desired. Apropos of the questions that have been asked in the past by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) and the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Spencer), we must come to the point and ask ourselves what could be the effect of the proposed bill? It could give the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) authority to deal with complaints concerning discrimination in employment which in all other respects is subject to the civil service commission and to the Civil Service Act. We know the jurisdiction of the industrial inquiries commission appointed by the Minister of Labour. I therefore come back to the point I brought to the attention of the house previously, namely the fact that the civil service commission reports directly to the house and not through the minister. For this reason, if we proceed as proposed by the hon. member for Skeena, we could quite conceivably be setting up a great conflict in jurisdiction. I reiterate that which I have repeated time and time again. The desired results could be and should be brought about by an amendment to the Civil Service Act.
Another thing I should like to draw to the attention of the house relates to some of the general provisions in the bill of rights. The right of the individual to liberty comes in clause 1 of this bill. The right of the individual to liberty comes in part I of the bill of rights. I think it is obvious to all hon. members that the principle of fair employment must apply equally to all Canadians. I realize only too well that I am arguing in a very indirect fashion at this time, but liberty must have economic aspects. Many members on both sides of the house have brought up this question time and time again. The liberty to be employed fairly should apply equally to all Canadians. I think I am not letting my imagination run away with me when I say that these provisions of the bill of rights have a direct bearing on the question we are discussing this afternoon.
I should repeat that which I said at the beginning of my remarks this afternoon. It almost seems unnecessary to put written legislation in such detail on the statute books because the principles of non-discrimination

Private Bills
are written so largely within the hearts of the Canadian people. Because such provisions are provided in the bills of rights and because the civil service commission actually is following a policy of non-discrimination and because these ends can better be achieved by amendments to the Civil Service Act I do not think we should accept this bill.
The hon. member for Skeena said he had made numerous phone calls to members of the civil service commission or to members of the civil service in this regard and they had told him that perhaps this was not the case. My opinion is, after speaking to members of the administration, that is the official point of view, and that these ends would better be achieved by amendments to the Civil Service Act.
I might be considered to be straying from the subject but I know that if some hon. members opposite run true to form I will be classed among those who are said to be talking out the bill. Such is not the case. In the hour between five and six o'clock very often bills are not passed but I believe that the private members' hour is a most valuable one because much information is put before the government and many views are aired which eventually bring about good legislation.
I have discussed my point of view in relation to a most important subject. Just because I am not in favour of the immediate passage of the bill as it now stands, I hope no one will feel that I tolerate discrimination in any shape or form. I simply do not believe that as the bill now stands it will help to correct the situation, one which I believe the government can perhaps correct in a better way through the amendments I have discussed. In my opinion the bill seeks to correct a situation which exists only in the imaginations of certain members and other people. If you see discrimination in any particular instance, point it out. I believe that you will not find it in the past or present and I sincerely hope, as a Canadian, that you will never find it in the future.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to speak on Bill No. C-9 and also to express sentiments which I hold on the subject of non-discrimination. It is my view, as has already been said by the speakers who have preceded me, that there is no feeling on the part of anyone that there should be discrimination.
Having said that, it is my view that Bill C-9 serves no useful purpose. It is unnecessary. The matter has already been taken care of. There is no case or example of discrimination in the civil service before us and therefore I find it impossible to support the bill. I might add that a similar bill has been before the

house for debate on three different occasions and each time advanced by the same sponsor. I have checked the records and I find that no other member of the C.C.F. or new party group other than the sponsor has spoken on the bill. I am wondering whether he has any support from that corner of the house for this measure.
I have already indicated that existing legislation covers the situation. If that is true, and I shall attempt to show that it is, I wonder why the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) has insisted on bringing this bill forward on so many occasions. I should like to ask him what his motives were in bringing the bill forward.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE
speechtext: Motives of decency.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO CIVIL SERVICE
speechtext:
I wonder whether there are not deeper motives behind the bill, whether it is not perhaps designed to win votes in his riding or to gain some particular end that he is seeking to achieve. He has not disclosed these things and we can only surmise. However, I will take the bill just as it is and speak on this subject because in my opinion it is important. I am in agreement with the principle of nondiscrimination and, as the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) said, good should come out of this debate. Each speaker will have an opportunity to express himself and from that some good is bound to come.
I should like to quote from the speech made by the hon. member for Skeena on February 19, 1960 when he introduced a similar bill. As found on page 1271 of Hansard, he said:
The bill which is before the house is very short. It merely seeks to make the present Canada Fair Employment Practices Act applicable to Her Majesty, her servants and agents of Her Majesty, or, in effect, applicable to the civil service and to employees in the government service. This, of course, does not suggest that with regard to the employment of civil servants there exists at the present time any such discrimination because of the factors that I set out earlier. In fact, I think I can say without any contradiction or any qualification that no such discrimination enters into the employment of candidates for the civil service.
Note these words from the mouth of the sponsor of the bill:
In fact, I think I can say without any contradiction or any qualification that no such discrimination enters into the employment of candidates for the civil service.
He says there is none and yet he wants this particular measure applied to the civil service. For what reason? The present Civil Service Act is designed to take care of the problem if it should arise. The hon. member did not refer to any particular case. If the hon. member could point to some incident where an individual had been discriminated against by the civil service authorities or by some department of the government then we would have a case before us and something

to debate and get our teeth into. But here we are talking in the abstract. We are being asked to pass a piece of legislation and make it applicable to the civil service when it has no particular applicability. We are not correcting anything. There is no case before us to show there has been any discrimination within the civil service. I should like to refer to the Civil Service Act, chapter 48 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. Section 19 reads as follows:
Except where otherwise expressly provided, all appointments to the civil service shall be upon competitive examination under and pursuant to this act, and shall be during pleasure; but no appointment, whether permanent or temporary, shall be made to a local position within a province, and no employee shall be transferred from a position in a province to a local position in the same or in another province, whether permanent or temporary, until and unless the candidate or employee has qualified by examination ...
In section 25 we find the following:
1.	Competitive examinations shall be held by the commission to establish lists of persons eligible for appointment.
2.	Such examinations may be written or oral or in the form of a demonstration of skill or any combination of these, and they shall be of a character fairly to test and determine the relative fitness and ability of candidates actually to perform the duties of the class to which they seek to be appointed, and any investigation of training and experience and any test of technical knowledge, manual skill, or physical fitness that, in the judgment of the commission, serves to this end may be employed.
In other words, the situation seems to be working very well under the Civil Service Act as it now stands. These examinations are open to everyone. There is a clause in the act which entitles war veterans to a preference, and I am sure everyone agrees with that. The Civil Service Act cannot be construed as containing any discrimination. The very essence of non-discrimination can be read between the lines in all parts of this act. Having worked as a civil servant for the federal government for a short time myself, I realize that what every civil servant wants is security. He wants to have good working conditions and he likes to be doing a job that he feels is important. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if this bill were enacted it would do nothing to assist the present civil servant in the discharge of his duties or improve his life as a civil servant. In other words, the passage of this bill will not benefit present civil servants.
The purpose of the bill, therefore, must be to provide for non-discrimination in the hiring of new civil servants. On a previous occasion the sponsor of this bill made a statement that it is not possible to legislate against the state of mind. I thoroughly agree with him on that point. It is impossible to legislate to cover the way in which a person will act
Private Bills
when he is acting as a result of a state of mind. In other words, his intolerance or discrimination may be the result of acting by intuition. Certainly the bill which is before us would not help in preventing that individual from acting according to his state of mind. If this bill were enacted it would not prevent intolerance or discrimination. I think a better approach to the situation would be from the point of view of education. In this way people can be shown that we are all created equal and that, given the opportunity, each one performs different skills equally well.
In drawing my remarks to a close, I want to say again that in so far as this bill is concerned the matter is already covered by the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. This act takes care of the problem in so far as industry is concerned. The Civil Service Act takes care of the problem in so far as civil servants are concerned. If a revision of the Civil Service Act is to be undertaken, perhaps this matter could be referred to the committee dealing with the matter and, in this way, the question of discrimination could be given proper and thorough consideration.
I have already made the point that it is not possible to legislate in connection with a state of mind. Another point is that no evidence has been brought forward to indicate there has been discrimination in any particular segment of the civil service. In my view, this fact relieves the house of any necessity for taking immediate action. I conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by saying that I must, because of the unnecessary aspect of this bill, cast my vote against it at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to participate in the debate on this Bill No. C-19. At the outset, I may say I am in favour of the provisions of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. However, my position on the bill before us this afternoon is along the lines of the positions of previous speakers we have heard today. I may say I am rather disappointed that the sponsor of this bill did not see fit to make a statement at the commencement of this debate to bring us up to date on his views on the bill. I am disappointed also that no other member of the C.C.F. has taken part in the debate thus far, especially since they are now members of the New Democratic party and their views may have changed somewhat from those previously held. It is disappointing also to see that the Liberal party has not participated in this debate. I suppose the members of that party feel the bill is rather superfluous because the interest they

Private Bills
are showing is very small. I believe there are only three members of that group sitting in the house at the moment.
However, since the sponsor of the bill has not made a statement, I think the words he used in introducing the bill, as they are found at page 1270 of Hansard for February 19, 1960, might be usefully repeated. He said:
The Canada Fair Employment Practices Act came into effect on July 1, 1953 and, in short, it provides that no employer shall discriminate in so far as the employment of employees or the terms or conditions of employment are concerned because of race, national origin, colour or religion. The act also prevents an employer from using the facilities of a hiring agency which discriminates on grounds of race, national origin, colour or religion, and it provides, further, that a trade union shall not discriminate against its members or prevent potential members from becoming members of that union, and that it shall not expel them from the union on grounds of race, national origin, colour or religion. The act also prevents a trade union expelling a member because he lodges a complaint under this particular measure. Procedures are described, and penalties are provided for infringement.
As I stated at the beginning, I am wholeheartedly in favour of this act as I am sure are most of the members of this house. The hon. member who preceded me mentioned that the sponsor of this bill had indicated that he had no knowledge of any discrimination within the civil service to which this bill is primarily directed and he gave a quotation. I should also like to give a quotation, but a different one. It is from page 477 of the debates of the House of Commons of the session of 1960-61, volume 1, and is as follows:
I am quite sure, and there Is no shadow of a doubt in my mind-and I am sure there is no shadow of a doubt in the mind of anyone in this house-that the intent of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act is followed by the civil service commission in its function of employing people. I am also quite sure that no discrimination exists on these bases whatsoever.
Therefore I believe the sponsor himself has admitted that the bill is rather superfluous. As the hon. member who preceded me has stated, if there were in the civil service any examples of discrimination, he certainly could have a basis for arguing for and supporting this bill.
As I stated, the chief purpose of this bill is to extend the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act to bind Her Majesty in right of Canada and the servants and agents of Her Majesty in right of Canada. At the present time I believe that crown corporations are also covered under this act. Section 3 (m) reads as follows:
3.	This act applies to and in respect of employment upon or in connection with any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, including, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing,.. .

(m) the employment by any corporation established to perform any function or duty on behalf of the government of Canada of employees.
Therefore this bill seems to restrict itself primarily to the civil service and I should like to make some remarks in this connection. As has already been stated by most of the members, I believe the civil service commission has always followed the policy of no discrimination. I do not believe they have ever transgressed the principles that are laid down in the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act in so far as race, colour or religion are concerned. Any difference in treatment of applications can be attributed to national origin which has been imposed by requirements of the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
As has already been stated by a number of those who have spoken, the civil service commission have seen fit to modify their application forms where it has been found that any of the questions contained therein do not comply with the provisions of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. I believe they are always vigilant in this regard and that wherever possible they remove any question which may carry any hint of any discrimination in hiring for the civil service of Canada.
There is one thing that I should like to bring out. If this act were to come into effect the situation would be this. In essence, under the provisions for the review of infringements I believe there is set up an industrial disputes commission or industrial inquiry commission and that the recommendations of this commission may be made final and binding through orders issued by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr). In other words, at the present time any infringement of the Civil Service Act would be dealt with by the civil service commission which reports directly to parliament and not to any minister. Thus any disputes which may arise are removed from any political influence. If this act were to come into effect it would in essence place the binding decision with respect to any dispute in the hands of the minister. Knowing the Minister of Labour whom I consider to be a good friend and for whom I have a high regard, I might say that in some instances the decision he might reach might be even more just than one that could be reached by the civil service commission. None the less, to me it is strange that the sponsor of this bill would wish that this happen. I am sure that he would be one of the last ones to deny that the civil service commission should be completely free from any act of political interference or jurisdiction.
As I have stated, there is a modification of terms in the application forms of the civil

service commission; and I believe that the act which is being revised at the present time will perhaps go even further in changing some of the requirements for admission to the civil service. I am thinking particularly of that specification which limits applicants to British subjects with five years residence in Canada. It is my own hope-and I hope my feeling is shared by members of the government-that perhaps this requirement can be changed in order to give Canadians any preference that may be given under the act.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we adjourned the debate at five o'clock, I was just about to state that Canada is quite right in promoting negotiations to the extreme limit in view of the international issues to be settled.
But those negotiations should be effected, as was stated by several members who preceded me, firmly, wisely and with unity between members of the alliance. And that unity which the allies must strengthen further will only be achieved by greater mutual confidence. Now, that confidence will not be generated in isolation, but in co-operation and by a co-ordination of all efforts.
That is why I submit that the stand of this government in respect of such organizations as NATO and NORAD is the wisest stand possible. For instance, I think that in view of this collective defence, the 14 NATO nations will have to draw more closely together to establish among themselves that mutual trust which will enable them to form a solid bloc so that negotiation can be as efficient as possible with regard to the objectives to be achieved.
Supply-National Defence
Since the Soviet government resumed its nuclear tests and since our southern neighbours decided to counter with similar tests, though theirs are underground and laboratory tests, the Canadian people shiver with apprehension and wonder what this country has in terms of civil defence.
Before coming back here for the second part of the session I found that several citizens from that fine riding of Sherbrooke, which is perhaps not familar to you, Mr. Chairman, but which, like many other ridings in this country, is composed of peaceful Canadians who want only to prosper in the sun in all dignity and freedom, were worrying about what they should do for their protection in the event of a nuclear attack and with regard to the damaging effects of strontium 90, of which a fall-out has again been noted following the resumption of the tests.
According to the information secured, we know that an order in council was enacted in May 1959 which resulted in a general revision of the duties and the powers relating to civil protection.
That order in council provided that it would be up to the Department of National Defence to set up a warning system for the public, to determine the site of nuclear explosions, to make an estimation of the damages and of the number of victims, to control, supervise and carry out the return operations into the stricken areas, and to give emergency support to municipal and provincial authorities for the maintenance of law and order. The Department of National Health and Welfare was given the responsibility of helping municipalities and provinces set up plans providing for medical and public health emergency services as well as plans for emergency housing, emergency food supplies and welfare.
Through the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) has been entrusted with the maintenance of law and order, as well as the control and the direction of traffic in case of emergency. Finally, through the emergency measures organization, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) has assumed the responsibility for co-ordinating the planning of civil protection at the federal level, for helping provincial and municipal authorities in the preparation of security plans and for keeping in touch with provincial governments and other countries in the matter of civil protection.
In addition to the foregoing, other government departments have emergency duties to perform in fields that normally come under their jurisdiction.

Supply-National Defence
For instance, in a state of emergency, the Department of Agriculture, would advise farmers on what they should do to protect their cattle and their crops against radioactive fall-about. The department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission would look after emergency control of labour and the Department of Defence Production would set up a skeleton organization which would attend to essential supplies.
On the provincial level, organizations have been established which correspond in general to the federal E.M.O. Those provincial units are concerned with planning for the uninterrupted operation of government at the provincial level; they also help in the implementation of plans to ensure the survival of local communities.
Even though emergency planning involves numerous problems, major progress has been made these last few years, and especially during the past months, as far as the implementation of the plans to guarantee the maintenance of government and the survival of the people in case of emergency.
Already the federal government has started the building of regional headquarters where, in the event of a nuclear war, parts of the federal and provincial governments could operate.
As far as communications are concerned, an organization called the national emergency telecommunication organization has been set up in order to insure the security of communication systems, to provide for replacement routes in danger zones and to stockpile mobile and stationary equipment.
The Department of Defence Production has made considerable progress in the establishment of its war supply agency and it has opened a number of regional offices throughout the country to help in that matter.
In the field of transportation planning, the establishment of skeleton organizations in the provinces is recommended; their task would be to control the use of commercial highway transportation in time of war.
The Department of National Health and Welfare is actively working towards its objective, which is to stockpile medical supplies in premises scattered throughout the country. About $10 million were provided to that end and a number of improvised 200-bed hospitals are to be placed at the disposal of the provinces for emergency cases.
The Department of National Defence has made great progress in the setting up of a warning system for the public with the installation of sirens in key locations and the establishment all across the country of warning centres with a full-time staff.

The drawing up of fall-out shelter plans for private homes has been one of the main undertakings of the federal E.M.O.
The organization also looks after training and frequently offers courses both in various areas and at the civil defence college in Arnprior, maintained and administered by the Department of National Health and Welfare. Those courses have been attended by federal and provincial representatives, and also by mayors and reeves of several hundreds of municipalities in Canada. In Sherbrooke, the municipal authorities recently selected Colonel Sarto Roy to attend those courses.
Contacts between this organization and local civil defence organizations are also provided for otherwise.
To sum up, I should say that very great progress has been accomplished in the field of emergency measures, and this is why we are able to conclude that the Canadian population has every reason to have confidence in the present administration of this country. The vision of our leaders and their carefulness should lead us to do so.
Before closing my remarks, I should like to put one humble suggestion to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) which might also be put to the cabinet as a whole. It has to do with civil defence. Could not the Department of National Defence and the government consider the possibility of including in their winter works program the development of underground parking lots in municipalities where the population is more than 25,000? Such a project would achieve two objectives. In the civic field, it would alleviate parking and traffic problems in larger cities. In regard to civil defence, those underground parking lots, suitably organized from the standpoint of health and food services, would, in my humble opinion, accommodate adequately the people who would have to take cover in case of emergency.
