speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister reminded us this morning that this was his first presentation of the estimates of the department since he assumed the most important portfolio of Minister of National Defence. I should like to begin my remarks by extending to him my very best wishes on this very important occasion. I should like also to join with him in the tribute he paid to his predecessor whom we all respect as a gallant soldier and as a gentleman and whom we still remember with a great deal of regard and affection.

The minister told us this morning that we are living in a time of stress. He referred particularly to the threat of Soviet domination and the threat of force to attain that domination which overshadows us at the present time and which is indicated in the resumption of the testing of nuclear bombs.
It has been interesting to hear some hon. members draw a parallel between the use of nuclear weapons and the use of gas in the last war. In my opinion a true parallel cannot be drawn. It is true that both sides in the last war had the capability of using gas and of engaging in bacteriological warfare, yet neither side actually did so. Both sides refrained; but that I think was because each side was waiting for the other to start. If we are going to draw an exact parallel with respect to nuclear warheads we must somehow come to a decision in regard to the use of nuclear tactical weapons. While our parallel is based mainly on our thinking about strategic nuclear weapons, the line between tactical nuclear weapons and strategic nuclear weapons is very thin and it is getting thinner with every new scientific development. Therefore, unless we do come to some understanding and agreement about the use of nuclear weapons for tactical purposes, then it is quite possible that the parallel will break down and one side may be tempted to use tactical weapons with nuclear warheads to offset the disadvantage of inferior numbers.
The minister told us also that this threat of Soviet domination was being implemented on many fronts. He listed the economical and political, the ideological and the military fronts. He told us that to combat it counteraction was required in all these areas. To my knowledge this is the first time that any minister has openly acknowledged the importance of the ideological factor and the need for ideological counter-measures.
Hon. members are well aware of my interest in this aspect of national defence; therefore they will understand my disappointment that today the minister chose to confine himself solely to the military aspect of our defence policy. It is well known that the military leaders of the U.S.S.R. and the Chinese republic put the ideological factor first. To them this is paramount and everything else, including economic policy and strategy, military policy and strategy and political manoeuvres, is subordinated to ideological considerations.
In the debate on the estimates of this department last year I made extended reference to this matter, as can be found in Hansard
Supply

National Defence of August 5, at page 7619, and I do not intend to repeat what I said on that occasion. I merely wish to call to the attention of the minister the words of Air Vice Marshal Traill, who said:
The war of arms, if it comes, is an extension of the ideological war. At the higher levels, military and ideological strategy are one. Together they form the strategy of this world conflict. If we wish to survive it is madness to consider one in isolation from the other. The enemy is very clear on this. He is equally prepared to take an ideological or a military initiative, to use an ideological or a military weapon.
Since these words come from such an eminent military authority, I think they should be given very serious consideration. I ask the minister to do this and I express the hope also that he will have something more to say on this important subject later on in this debate. At the same time I should like to compliment the minister on the ideological awareness which he has displayed on several occasions since taking office. That awareness is evident also in the statement he made this morning in his reference to the ideological implications of unilateral disarmament and of peaceful coexistence which, in my opinion, is an effective answer to those who urged coexistence upon us in the debate which took place a few days ago.
We have Mr. Khrushchev's own words about peaceful coexistence, and I should like to put them on record at this time. Mr. Khrushchev has spoken a hundred times on peaceful coexistence. The most precise definition he has given of it appeared in a speech he delivered at Novosibrisk some time ago. He said:
Peaceful coexistence must be properly understood. It represents a continuation of the struggle between two social systems, but a struggle carried on by peaceful means, without war and without interference in the internal affairs of other countries. For us it is an economic, political and ideological struggle, not a trial of military strength.
The plain fact is that peaceful coexistence does not mean peace but struggle, and we would do well to follow the minister's lead and explain this to our people at every opportunity.
The minister also told us this morning that the cornerstone of Canada's foreign policy was collective security based on a system of alliances as signified by NATO, NORAD and the United Nations organization. He pointed out:
The strength of union is the sum of the individual members.
And also:
Only so long as the will of the individual member remains steadfast will the coalition be strong and its will to stand together be abundantly clear to any would be aggressor.

Supply-National Defence
These two statements which I have quoted in the reverse order from which the minister made them point up the need for a positive unifying force in NATO. At present we are unified in NATO mainly by fear, by fear of the threat that faces us, but fear is never satisfactory as a source of unity, as we know from our experience in the last world war. Many nations then bound themselves together and called themselves united nations but as soon as the immediate threat disappeared the unity disappeared along with it. In my opinion maximum unity cannot be attained until we have worked out a clear-cut ideological objective which will challenge the communist and non-communist world alike.
Last year I advocated the setting up of an ideological strategy board which I outlined on page 7623 of Hansard, and I again ask the minister to give consideration to this suggestion.
All hon. members regardless of party will find themselves in full agreement with the two objectives outlined by the minister this morning, namely peace by preventing war and the prevention of our subjection to a foreign power. To these I should like to add a third objective, namely that we should work together to create a new moral climate from which a true and lasting peace can result. In the debate that was concluded yesterday we heard something about the lessons of history. The lessons of history teach us that peace never follows disarmament. That was the lesson of world war I and world war II. True disarmament can only follow a true peace and a true peace can only result from a climate which develops out of the practice of moral values.
Although general objectives are convenient for the purpose of making a brief summary or for giving a broad outline of policy, I feel it would be more helpful and certainly more conducive to an orderly debate if these general objectives could be broken down into a number of specific objectives. For the benefit of the committee I have listed a number of objectives which in my opinion should comprise a defence policy for Canada. I should like to place them on the record in the following order:
1.	To maintain a strong, healthy and sound economy capable of withstanding economic attack and of providing at the same time a strong economic base for a total defence effort.
2.	Within the limits of manpower and economic capacity, to make the maximum contribution of men, machines and weapons for the defence of Canadian territory by land, sea and air against any aggressor.

3.	To defend the Canadian people against ideological penetration and aggression.
4.	To develop and maintain the highest possible morale both among the armed forces and the civilian population; to develop the will to resist aggression, to survive and to win.
5.	Within the limits of manpower and economic capacity (a) to make the maximum contribution to the continental defence system of North America through NORAD; (b) to make the maximum contribution to the defence of the rest of the free world through NATO; (c) to meet our commitments and obligations to the United Nations organization and to increase its effectiveness.
6.	To maintain a fully mobile force of the order of a brigade group that can be put at the disposal of the United Nations to help extinguish small brush-fire wars before they can develop into big ones.
7.	To develop and maintain an adequate program of civil defence, including defence against nuclear flash and fall-out, together with the necessary organization of personnel and equipment to make it effective.
8.	To promote the fall-out shelter as the symbol of our will to survive.
9.	To offset the "Maginot line" psychology engendered by defence thinking, planning and training and by means of ideological training to enable both service personnel and civilian population to go on the offensive and take ideological initiatives. This is the only area where offensive action is possible but it is a most vital one.
10.	To maintain a proper balance of manpower and materials as between defence requirements, including defence industries, and civilian requirements so that the one will not undermine the other or impair the economy as a whole.
11.	To achieve the best defence value for every defence dollar.
12.	To preserve-I think this is most important-the prestige and honour of service in defence of one's country as one of the highest and noblest professions.
While there might be no disagreement with the general objectives stated by the minister there might be room for disagreement as to specific objectives and the methods by which they may be attained. In particular, I think there is room for disagreement as to the means of making the maximum contribution. It is open to question whether Canada's maximum contribution can be made best through more up-to-date and efficient equipment or through increased manpower as the minister advocated this morning.

I think there is also some room for disagreement whether we are really getting the best value for the defence dollar. Certainly when we look to the role of the navy there is room for doubt, in spite of what the minister told us this morning, that we are really getting the best defence for our tax dollar. It is true that the minister is going to man the navy to full strength but those destroyers are not capable of dealing with the type of submarines now possessed by the enemy. Certainly if we are going to place emphasis again on the use of conventional weapons we must think more about the conventional role, and the types of warships that we have at the present time are not very useful in this regard.
I think that the government should give more consideration to the use of hydrofoil vessels for naval purposes, as they are now developed to the point where they can deal more effectively with submarines and can be used for the rapid transportation of troops and equipment. I think possibly we should also be thinking about the use of killer submarines.
There is no doubt in my mind that we cannot obtain the maximum value for the tax dollar until our services are completely unified at the top operational level. Here I wish to point out that I am not talking about the kind of unification we have had so far which has resulted in an increase in personnel rather than a decrease. While I am on the subject of the tax dollar, I should like to draw to the committee's attention the parallel of Sweden. Sweden is a small country with a population of 7.5 million people. Her defence budget for 1960 was the equivalent of $550 million, Canadian, and that is comparable to an expenditure for Canada of $1,320 million. This year we are spending something of the order of $1,600 million.
For Sweden's $1,320 million, this is what the people get. They have an army of 250,000 troops, 14 divisions of first line troops; an air force of 1,000 first line aircraft, most of which are interceptors and ground attack fighters. For the navy, Sweden gets approximately the same number of ships as the Royal Canadian Navy, but uses only about one third the number of personnel we do. They will soon have included in their navy 33 modern submarines, some of which have anti-sub capabilities.
In so far as civil defence is concerned, for an expenditure of about $200 million, Canadian, in 1958 and declining to $55 million in 1960, the Swedish government is providing
Supply-National Defence the nation with civil defence measures which include not only warning, information, fall-out shelters, evacuation plans, and re-entry organizations but also blast shelters in literally every city over 50,000 people. Over one half million Swedes have been given intensive civil defence training in one role or another. Every new building in Sweden includes a fall-out shelter costing about 2 per cent of the over-all construction cost. People living in older buildings pay toward the cost of public blast shelters which are nearby for their use.

Mr. Chairman, I consider it a great honour and privilege to take some small part in this debate on the subject of Canadian defence. I take a great personal interest in Canada's defence and am not ashamed to stand and speak about it because I was a volunteer in the last great war. I do not relish the thought of a third great war. Nevertheless after reading the newspapers and hearing reports from abroad, I could not be sure that the third great war has not already started. We certainly have got to the point in international blackmail where it is hard for a man with red blood in his veins to sit idly by while our children and our children's children are poisoned from the skies in a cynical fashion. If the Russians do not know that this is a war against humanity, then it is time every free man in the world stood up and said what it is. Whether we have to retaliate in kind now or later, we do not know. We pray it may never come.
Let me take you back a thousand years or so for a few moments because if there is any
use in reading history, it is to try to learn some of the lessons which history has to give manking. I take you back to the days of Ancient Greece. Ancient Greece was a medium sized nation like Canada, these people were by and large simple, decent people who like to work in the lumberwoods and to sail the seas. They were in short industrious and free men. A great nation called Persia wished to extend her empire into Greece. Amongst the Greeks in those days, as in Canada today, there were many well meaning persons who hated war and who preached pacifism, tolerance and brotherhood; and well they might do so. But this did not deter Persia. Persia amassed an army of 10 million men. She moved down on little Greece and as she came, city after city offered gifts of earth and water which were the symbols of subservience. Athens, the greatest of Greek cities, was civilized. She liked ease, luxury and pleasure. She had those things. She was offered a dishonourable peace and refused. The few who wanted to fight marched against the Persian host and those who did not want to fight waited at home. The few who fought, won. The Persian king could not understand his defeat and he asked those around him why Greece did not fall. Nobody could answer him. I think I can answer him. I think that character won and will always win.
The challenge today is the same as it was 3,000 years ago. We face this same disaster, if you like to call it that. But we do not have to go down to defeat. A bully and a slave never fights like a free man. I will go further than that and say that if you can convince this bully that you intend to fight like a free man, the chances are that you will never have to do so. I think that world war II started not in September of 1939 but at Munich. I hope that world war III has not already started. If it has not already started, I think it is time that all free men stood together and that they make it clear where they stand.
Some hon. members in this chamber have suggested getting out of NORAD. Why get out of NORAD? We cannot get out of NORAD. They say we lose sovereignty by being in NORAD. If we are not in NORAD we lose everything. There is no choice. Those who say we give up our sovereignty should read history as well. Let us go back once more for a lesson from Greek history. Athens, which was the greatest city in Greece, gave up leadership to her hated sister city Sparta in the war because she thought Sparta could carry arms better than she could. Victory was won again because Athens put freedom ahead of pride. As a Canadian I put freedom ahead of the pride of Canadians and say that if our great neighbour the U.S.A. has the armed

strength to deter nuclear war and the conventional strength to fight a conventional war, then I am going to be morally strong enough to stand beside them and for a short time share sovereignty with them. I am not afraid to share sovereignty with people who have never waged an aggressive war. Slow as they were to come into two wars which they did not start, they helped us in a magnificent fashion to finish them. I am not one who is afraid that even in a nuclear war or in a conventional war the slave nation which is Russia can whip the nation which is with us in our struggle to remain free.
To get down to hardware, may I say this. I have always stood for Canada being strong at home and generous abroad. She cannot be strong at home without the hardware. However, there is a limit to the price we can pay for the hardware. Those who argue about the value of the CF-105 and the CF-104 might well consider that when you are buying a child a rattle, if the rattle is made of diamonds and gold it cannot be afforded by a middle sized nation like us. I think the 104 aircraft is equal to if not superior in many ways to the 105. I have taken the trouble to go and see it. Our airmen have tested it. The airmen are glad to have it and I am proud to have some small part in providing them with this magnificent weapon. This weapon will also be built in Canada. It will be built by Canadair in Montreal. I would urge hon. members to go down there and see it being made. It is a magnificent weapon.
To those hon. members who say that this government has no defence policy, I say they are not abreast of the times. This government has and has always had a defence policy. That policy is to provide our people morally and physically with the weapons with which to defend freedom. However, we must do it within our economic structure. We are also going to build training planes in Canada. This is going to help our economy. It is going to balance our economy and add payroll to our working force. It is a proper and well thought out policy.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, may I say that I know where I stand, I know where my government stands, and I know where the great majority of the people of Canada stand.
I welcome what has been done as far as the government has gone. I can only hope that we expand our idea of national service and tell the young people of Canada and the old people also what it means to be a Canadian and that the price of freedom cannot come too high.

I should like to preface my remarks, Mr. Chairman, by offering my congratulations to the Minister of National Defence who, as he himself has said, is presenting his estimates to the house for the first time today. I should like to congratulate him upon the record he has shown in the very short time during which he has been Minister of National Defence. He has done a great deal to try to clear up a good many of the misapprehensions that exist in the country about problems respecting the defence of the nation and of the free world generally. In my view it is extremely important that this has been done. Perhaps in some way this debate will further help to clear the air in this regard.
I myself have found that there is more confusion in the minds of many Canadians concerning the matter of national defence than
8274	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence about any other single item of national import. One of the most obvious confusions I find is one that I have seen exemplified here during this debate, namely the confusion of the three fronts upon which the communist world advances upon us. As I see it, the communists challenge us on three separate sectors. First of all, as has been mentioned by many who have spoken, there is the ideological war in which they try to shape men's minds to accept the proposition that the communist form of government and the communist system of world order, in which all the nations would be brought under one dictatorship would provide the best future for the world. Second, there is the economic front. Many of those who have spoken here today have said that they think the most important fronts the communists have opened have been the ideological and economic ones. I feel that just as important as, or perhaps more important than either one of those attacks, and just as important as or more important than the hammer and sickle, the symbol of the communist ideology, is the red star, the symbol of the Russian army.
If we look at the record of accomplishments of the Russians in advancing in the world since 1945 we see they have accomplished much more by force of arms than by economic war or ideology. In 1945, when the rest of Russia's allies had disbanded their armies in the hope that freedom was safe for many centuries after the Nazis were defeated, the Russian army kept at full war strength. Despite their undertakings at Yalta in February, 1945, to allow the people in the countries over which their armies had run to have free elections, they forced upon a hundred million people in eastern Europe the slavery of communism.
I think it is very important to note that this was not done with ideology; it was done with the Russian army. Their stand there has been maintained not with ideology but under the red star of the Russian war machine. Communism is dangerous because it attacks men's minds. It is just as dangerous, or perhaps more directly dangerous, as the vehicle upon which Russian imperialism marches, supported always, everywhere in the world, by force of arms.
After 1945 the Russians kept 200 divisions under arms and with these divisions they gobbled up Poland, Hungary, Roumania, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Latvia, Estonia, Albania and Finland. Since that time, as I have said, their most important successes have been with armies. They occupied North Korea while at the same time the southern

part of Korea was occupied by the armies of our allies. An agreement was reached that Korea would be vacated as soon as the country seemed able to look after itself. The Russians took advantage of their time there to build up a communist army in North Korea, and when South Korea was vacated by the forces of freedom they engineered an attack upon that country. In the Berlin blockade of 1948 they sought to force their way upon the people of that city with armies, not with ideology. Their present threat to free Berlin is a simple threat of force.
While we must always be ready to defend democracy and to push forward our ideals and spiritual beliefs in the world, on the ideological and economic fronts, I think it is a great mistake, and one under which many people labour, that we can with ideological and economical warfare alone meet the Russian threat.
Until NATO was formed in 1949 we had no chance in Europe. I am sure that if NATO had not been formed at that time and developed since then into the very powerful force it is today, all Europe would be under the Russian heel.
I talked very recently to a senior diplomat from a European country which has had some experience with the communist army. He told me that from his 30 years in diplomacy and from his observations of wars and rivalries between countries he was convinced that if we had not the armed strength we now have the Russians would have no hesitation in attacking us. He said the Russians would knock this nation and any other free nation flat to accomplish their aims if they were not afraid to do so.
I think it is from that point of view that we must face any question of national defence of Canada and the part we play with our allies to marshal the NATO nations and the other unconquered nations of the world against this Soviet threat. When NATO was taken over by General Eisenhower as Supreme Allied European Commander in 1950 it was very weak indeed. All that was left of allied forces in Europe were some 12 divisions, mostly administrative and occupation forces, some 400 aircraft, 400 ships and a few airfields. Yet, as I have said, the Russian army was at full strength. Since then, by acting together in NATO and by realizing that only by standing together can we stand at all, we have built up an army in Europe that is considered quite capable of stopping any advance by the Russian army with conventional arms in Europe.
It is true that it is not of the strength of the Russian conventional force, but when it is considered that many more times the force or power will be needed to attack than to

defend, it is felt by most people informed in military affairs that the NATO force in Europe would be successful in stopping a Russian advance.
However, the NATO shield has to be further built up. It will cost us money to do so, but I am one of those who feel that we must spend to develop our conventional forces as well as to assist where we can in the nuclear deterrent, if our nation is not to be seared by atomic war. No one can tell me that in weakness there is hope of avoiding war. That was the mistake of 1914 and of 1939.
I feel that the chief hope for safety in our country, and in the other nations of the free world with whom we are allied, is the great nuclear deterrent force we have at the present time. I feel it is incumbent upon us as members of NATO and in partnership with the United States of America to maintain that striking force where we can and to do everything possible to see we are not at the mercy of Russian military nuclear might by default.
Many people ask me why Canada does not develop its own deterrent force and why it must rely upon nations like the United States. Or perhaps they have read books like Mr. Minifie's "Peacemaker or Powder Monkey" and have been led to subscribe to the thought that we would be better off to go it alone as a neutralist in the world. We might thereby pick up leadership and prestige which otherwise we would not have. It seems to me if, as Mr. Minifie and other people suggest, we spend our money to assist other nations to fight only the ideological and economic war, we would leave ourselves open very soon to the devasting attack of the Russian military force. It is recognized by all hon. members in this house that we Canadians cannot afford to contribute to or to maintain any sort of deterrent force. I suppose if we could and if we had the capacity to do that as has the United States of America, it would be our moral obligation to try to equip and maintain a deterrent force of our own since only behind such a force is there protection for the free world.
We cannot afford to do that. We have been told today by the Minister of National Defence that it would have cost over $2 billion to put the Avro Arrow aircraft into squadron production, and when we hear of the prices paid by the United States to develop missiles and so on, it is obvious that we cannot afford to be in the big race; we cannot maintain direct deterrent forces. We can, however, do something to help protect that deterrent so it is available for retaliation in case it is needed. We can do something to make sure the deterrent force is there to discourage an 90205-6-522J
Supply-National Defence enemy from daring to launch the weapons of atomic war upon the free world.
With our radar system in this country we are now assisting in the warning of a missile or bomber attack. We can with interceptors and with the Bomarc missile help stop an attack on this nation or this continent. The argument has been put forward that the Bomarc and interceptors are not the final answer to an attack by Russia, and therefore we should make no attempt at all to meet the threat from that quarter. It has been said that the manned bomber is disappearing, and indeed I believe it is, and therefore we are wasting money if we cannot stop both missiles and bombers with weapons of the nature of the Bomarc or present day interceptors. It seems to me that the Hawker Hurricane and the Spitfire were not the final answer either to the defence of England in 1940, but they helped. The Bomarc anti-bomber missile and the interceptor will help defend us and the day may come when we will require all the defensive fire power we can find. It also seems to me that if we did not try to defend against the manned bomber we would be inviting an enemy to attack us with a very much cheaper and more readily available weapon than the intercontinental ballistic missile.
I should like to read an excerpt from a speech made by Dr. J. E. Keyston, vicechairman, defence research board, which I think very neatly sets forth Canada's position with regard to the Bomarc and interceptor defence against the manned bomber. Dr. Keyston said:
Let me now turn from broad defence policy considerations to a specific point of controversy that springs up when any reference is made to our defences against bomber aircraft.
It seems that everyone knows we are rushing rapidly into the missile age, and that in the next decade Russia is more likely to be producing intercontinental ballistic missiles than long range bombers. So why put any more money into defences against bombers? I am not going to involve myself in all the facets of this question and their answer, but I would make the following observation. If we are to deter Russia from attacking, NATO must provide a deterrent that is balanced. I can think of no better way of encouraging Russia to use missiles as the threat and bombers for the actual surprise attack, than by our deciding she will not use bombers and our allowing NATO's bomber defences to decay.
So long as the military game remains that of frightening Russia as much as she frightens us, the NATO alliance has to keep as up to date as Russia does in capacity for attack and capacity for defence in relation to all modem weapons. This is why, unhopeful as solution may appear, scientific research toward finding a defence against missiles must go on, and why research toward improvement of more conventional defence-and attack-must not be dropped. The Russians are not only very good scientists and engineers but they are outstanding chess players. Many a man, playing against the expert at chess, has kept his eye on his opponent's

Supply-National Defence pieces, only to suffer the humiliation of a checkmate by a miserable pawn that has been pushed through the defence.
It is also in the nature of a deterrent that it must not only be balanced but continuous. At any moment of time, one has to deter attack by the bombers, missiles, or other weapons available to the enemy at that time.
I submit that if the weapon sought by both the free and communist world is an antimissile missile the Bomarc "B" is at least a long step in that direction from the manned interceptor. If the defence of tomorrow is the anti-missile missile it seems reasonable that Canada should attempt to find out as much as she can about missile warfare and about defence against an enemy attack by missiles. Perhaps the great cost of an anti-missile missile may mean it will never be developed. However some day there might well be a defence against nuclear attack by missile and it is more likely to be by anti-missile missile than by any other means. With the Bomarc our forces are being trained in the use of the weapons of today against manned bombers; some more advanced version of the Bomarc may be tomorrow a weapon against missiles that might attack from over the Arctic circle. Moreover if we are to maintain defensive installations in this country to protect our soil, purely defensive weapons that have no purpose but that of defence, I think they should carry all the punch they possibly can. The Bomarc is purely a defensive weapon. It has no offensive purpose whatever. It has a range of from 400 to 500 miles. There is no way it can be used to attack any other nation on our borders except, of course, technically the United States one might say. It cannot be used to launch an attack against the Soviet union. It is solely designed as a defensive weapon to knock down a bomber that might swoop down some night from high over the Arctic circle to attack our cities or the defence bases which house our deterrent force. If that time ever comes the weapons we send up to protect us should pack all the punch, nuclear or otherwise, that is available to us.
If we are equipping the Canadian forces with interceptors that are designed to meet, attack and destroy enemy bombers that are destined to turn our cities into ashes or to burn our countryside with nuclear blast, the aircraft should be armed with the most force that modern science can devise.
The argument is raised that if nuclear weapons are on our soil even for defensive purposes we must lose some of our sovereignty in having them here, in that they must be under the joint command of our nation and the United States. If the night ever comes when we wish to send a Bomarc missile or a Voodoo interceptor high into the 
sky to defend us, it would be a poor answer to the citizens of Canada to say that we were not properly armed because we feared some loss of sovereignty in so doing.
It is important to realize that for a generation we may be in the present stalemate. As long as there is no defence against nuclear attack it may well be that there will be no major war. Never in the history of humankind has a weapon been used in war, such as that available today, to which there is no defence, when both sides had this weapon. That is the present situation in world affairs. There is no complete defence to a nuclear attack except the threat of instant massive retaliation.
In the years ahead we have to be prepared to meet the challenge that Russia presents in terms of ideology and economic pressure. We must make the greatest sacrifices we can afford to make to counter this. We must do as much as we can to aid the underdeveloped nations in raising their standards of living and assuring them of their share of the world's blessings. We must harness our resources and square our shoulders to the burden of this quarter century. We must face the fact that we are confronted with a direct challenge from an enemy who knows no law and who will pull no punches in an effort to destroy us in his attempt to achieve world domination. While this situation confronts us we must be prepared as a first call upon our resources to defend our nation with modern arms, as modern arms threaten us. We should do more in terms of marshalling the will of the nation to that end. We have so many people who are willing to do what they can to assist nations that are not yet as highly developed as they should be and who are nevertheless highly confused with respect to defence. We must make every effort to make clear to them that the enemy is without, that some day we may need every resource at our command to defend our soil. It must be made clear that while we have no intention of attacking anybody, while we will make every effort to negotiate world problems and find peaceful solutions yet at the same time we are prepared to arm ourselves in kind against the force arrayed against us.

Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence have outlined in clear and unequivocal terms the position of the government with respect to defence policy and therefore I do not need to elaborate very much on my own views. However, I feel that the matter is of such importance that the people of this country are entitled to have placed on the record the views of the individual members of the committee.
One thing has become clear in the debate. I refer to the fact that the renewed threat of Soviet aggression has brought about on the question of defence policy a greater degree of unanimity than we have seen heretofore in this chamber. There was on the part of hon. members of the opposition a noticeable absence of statements such as were made by them not long ago to the effect that we should weaken our defence efforts in one way or another.
We have heard some statements of that kind coming, of course, from the C.C.F.-New party group. This is typical. I noticed this afternoon that the hon. member for Peterborough told us that we had nothing to learn from history. I do not know how many times we have to go over that, or how he expects us to learn in any other way than by looking back and seeing what has happened in the past. We do not need to look very far back through the pages of history to realize that if we are to survive in the world today we are going to have to be able to defend ourselves properly.
It has been said in the past that those who ignore the mistakes of history are condemned to repeat them. As I say, we do not need to look very far back through the pages of history to see what happens when we are not prepared to defend ourselves.
It has been said that sometimes we blunder into war because we have not had the proper international machinery for negotiations and, second, that we have not had a proper system of collective security. Well, since 1958 we have had both of those to a very great extent and I think the policy we have pursued since that time has been a very successful one. It was going along very successfully until we had spokesmen in various countries thinking it was going along so well that we could afford to weaken it. I am not at all convinced that it was not statements of this kind which have put us back in the position where we are now facing Soviet aggression once more.

It has been pointed out by many speakers in this debate that at the end of the second world war-one could go back further and learn the same lesson over again but we need to go back only that far to discover what happened-the western nations immediately disarmed, as we had done on previous occasions. We soon found out that the Soviet union had taken over the Baltic countries, parts of Finland, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Germany. Then, they went on to bring pressure to bear on Turkey and Iran when they did not want to take their troops out of there. Then, subversion was put on Hungary, Burgaria, Rumania, Poland and Czechoslovakia.
All of this happened when we were not in a position to defend ourselves; we did have international machinery for negotiation at that time. The United Nations had been formed but it became quite clear at that time that the United Nations alone was not able to give us security in the world. This situation obviously has not changed because we need to look back only to the time of Korea to see how useless the United Nations was at that time, or would have been, except for the fact that Russia had walked out and was not there to apply the veto which it did on every other occasion. In that particular instance the United Nations was able to take action, as I say, simply because of the fact that Russia had walked out of the meeting. Therefore, it becomes quite clear that if we are to survive we must have a collective system of security.
As I say, since the formation of NATO we have had that and it has been very successful. Therefore, when we come to discuss Canadian defence policy, in my opinion we can only discuss it in so far as we are a part of that system of collective security. It would be absolutely senseless to try to isolate it and I think far too much of this debate has been taken up in getting down to a very local level and a discussion of particular weapons which I do not think members of parliament are able to assess adequately. Surely, this is a matter for technical experts and for the government to decide, based on the advice given by those people who are in a position to make decisions of this kind.
We had a very good example in the speech made by the hon. member for Niagara Falls who read from newspaper editorials, and we learned how many ridiculous statements were made which were shown to be absolutely and completely unfounded. Statements of this kind which mislead the people of the country are very dangerous because if we are to succeed in our defence policy that policy must be freely understood and supported by all the people of this country.

However, as I say, it is important that the majority of Canadians understand the defence policy of the country, and what we are trying to do so that it will be fully supported and we shall not have statements of this kind made and the public misled as to exactly where we are going in our defence policy.
We have seen what has happened. I pointed out that in 1945, at the end of the second world war, we saw what happened when the Soviet union made the great advance it did because we had no collective security. Now NATO has provided that. As I say, we were going along very nicely. In fact we got going along too well and everybody started saying, "Now we can afford to weaken things a little bit, we have done so well." If the Soviet threat that is facing us now has done anything, surely at least it has awakened us again to the danger, and perhaps in the long run it may be a benefit to us, because I feel sure it will bring those nations closer together than they have been in the last two or three years.
I believe we are going to have to expand the deterrent weapons that we have, and have had during the past number of years. The policy has been, of course, to deter the Soviet union from attacking any of the North Atlantic treaty countries, or indeed any other country in the world, by having those forces necessary to be able to restrain them. I have some misgivings about the talk going on now with respect to building up conventional forces because it seems to me that if the Soviet union thought for one moment that we would be willing to fight what is now being referred to as a conventional war they probably would have no hesitation in starting one. I do not think there is any doubt that we would not be able to compete with them on those terms and would not be able to keep an army in the field in Europe that would fight with conventional weapons in order to deter them from aggression.
It has been the nuclear deterrent, mainly the strategic air command of the United States, that has in my opinion prevented the Soviet union from starting anything over the

past few years. I believe we would be making a mistake in giving the Soviet union any indication whatever that we are prepared to see them go into any country in the free world today and take it by force of arms if they can.
There has been a good deal of controversy over what are conventional weapons, because it is obvious that the Soviet forces .would have tactical nuclear weapons as they are called. Surely we would not want to put our men in the field to oppose them with so-called conventional weapons. On the other hand, if we equipped our forces with tactical weapons we obviously would not be able to fight a limited or conventional war. It is interesting to look at what the historians have to say about the last war when we talk about fighting a limited or conventional war. I came across a rather interesting statement today in a book by Stephen King-Hall entitled, "Our Times, 1900-1960". He discusses the aims of Hitler in 1939 and I should like to read one short sentence from page 190:
His immediate purpose in 1939 was to seize the western half of Poland in a short, limited war.
That war did not turn out to be very limited and I do not imagine that if a war should start now it would turn out to be very limited either. In any event, I do not see why we should give any consideration whatever to turning away from a policy which has been sound and successful over the past ten years. One would think the fact that it has been sound and successful in the past ten years would make us want to strengthen the concept under which we have been working. When John Foster Dulles was on the scene he made it quite clear that we were not going to accept aggression, that if the Soviet union attacked any free country in the world they were going to be subjected to a nuclear attack.
I am convinced that policy has worked and will continue to work provided we remain united, keep up to date and secure the proper weapons that are required. For that reason, before we start any campaign to build up conventional forces I think we should take a very careful look at the idea of suggesting to the enemy that we are willing to accept a conventional or any other kind of war. Surely that is only going to lead to trouble. It cannot have any other result. It is quite clear that a nuclear war means destruction for the entire world. It does not make any difference whether we want to call it a conventional war or a limited war. If the major powers become involved in the fighting then sooner or later tactical weapons are bound
Supply-National Defence to be introduced and then strategic weapons, if there is any differentiation between those two types of weapons.
For that reason I believe that if we are going to defend ourselves at all it is going to be by means of the nuclear deterrent and I believe that the nuclear deterrent must be spread among the NATO countries in so far as it is possible and that we cannot continue to rely mainly on the strategic air command of the United States. I am not saying that is all we have. There is a very large dispersal of armaments throughout the world now, but I think Canada is going to have to give consideration to whether the United States should have missile bases in this country. After all, we are on the side of the United States. There can be no mistake about that. I for one certainly reject any idea of placing Canada in any position of neutrality or trying to place the United States and the Soviet union in the same category. We can only be on the side of the United States. There is no other place for us to be.
If we are going to defend this country, then we must do so with every possible means at our disposal. It has already been pointed out that so far as nuclear weapons for Canada are concerned there may be some argument whether we should have strategic weapons of a missile nature in this country to act as a deterrent against Russia, but if the policy of deterrence is what we are going to follow then surely it is neither right nor reasonable for us to expect the United States to carry the brunt of such a policy and for us to sit back and say that it is all right for the United States to undertake everything and we will sit back and hope that they are going to be able to look after things. There may be an argument about whether or not we want to have weapons of this kind but, as has been said previously with regard to the Bomarc missile and weapons of that nature, weapons which cannot shoot beyond the borders of Canada, weapons which can do only one thing, shoot down an attacking airplane flying over our country, if we are going to antagonize by having nuclear warheads on these weapons I can only say that we are in such serious danger that it is not going to make any difference. If we are going to antagonize somebody by defending ourselves, I do not see what purpose there is in discussing the matter any further. Surely we are entitled to do that much. It will not harm anybody else for us to have that weapon on Canadian soil and I do not think we should have any hesitation whatever in making that decision.

I suggest that we should look at these matters in a realistic way rather than from the political point of view of saying those things which we think are going to appeal to our constituents at any given time. Some of the positions that have been taken by the Liberal party as they have jumped from one side of the field to the other have been rather remarkable. I can recall the Leader of the Opposition speaking in 1959 and talking about conventional wars. Then he dealt with tactical nuclear weapons. As found at page 7756 of Hansard, it will be seen that he was in favour of them. He thought they were a great thing, that our army should have them and that we should not expect our men to fight without them. However, by August 5, 1960 he had changed his mind and decided that we should not have them. I do not know whether that is political expediency but I want to say that I believe every hon. member has an obligation to put his views on the record because we may not have a second chance. If we make a mistake in what we are doing in trying to defend the free world today, we might not get another chance. In previous wars we have been able to blunder at the start and then, after the war was started, we have been able to build up our forces and eventually succeed. If there is another war, we are certainly not going to have that opportunity. When we consider this


question of defence, therefore, we want to make sure we do not make any mistakes.
Well, I am satisfied with the policy as outlined by the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence. I think the vast majority of Canadians are. However, I believe that it is the responsibility of all the members of the house to make sure that policy is spread across the country and that the people of this country understand it because misunderstanding and dissension can do a great deal of harm. There certainly is no room for political bickering. We have got to arrive at a common policy and with that policy we have got to stick. It is quite obvious if we are going to be a part of collective security, then we have at least got to have unanimity in our own country. For that reason, there is no sense in political bickering, especially when we are agreed on the broad general policies to be followed as was evident from the external affairs debate.
However, when we come to debate defence policy, then we find there are differences of opinion, mostly of a mind and nature as I pointed out, such as those concerning the individual weapons that are going to be used. Well, to put on a front of that kind does not help us very much when a united front, a determined front is one that is very important. The psychology of deterring the enemy is perhaps just as important as the weapons we have. We have many groups in the country that oppose a policy of deterrence. They are not large groups, but they can do nothing but aid and comfort the enemy and cause him to believe that perhaps we are not united enough to follow up the policy we have set. If the policy we have set is going to succeed, any potential aggressor has to be convinced we are going to carry out that policy; that we are not going to settle for something less or we are not going to back down at the last minute.
Many people have said that wars have started in the past because one side did not know what the other's intentions were. It has even been argued that if the United Kingdom had made its position clear earlier in 1939 we might not have had the second world war. We have to make sure there is no mistake about what our intentions are at the present time.
I have heard a number of members get up in this house and make that statement, but then by the time they finished speaking I was not quite sure what their intentions were. I do not know why we cannot get our intentions set out in plain terms so that not only we understand them but the other side understands them as well.
I suggest our policy has got to be, as it has been successfully for the past ten years,

that of a nuclear deterrent. We are not going to accept aggression on the part of the Soviet union. They have got to understand that we are not going to accept that aggression. They have to understand if there is going to be a war at all, it is going to mean destruction for them as well as ourselves and, therefore, war is absolutely unthinkable. In my view, that is the only policy that can succeed because it has been shown that negotiation alone cannot succeed. I doubt very much whether or not the United Nations would even be in existence today if it were not for NATO. The so-called uncommitted countries would not be in a position then to make the kind of statements they are making now. I am sure that Mr. Nehru would not have dared go to Moscow and say anything to Mr. Khrushchev if it were not for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization because he simply would not have been in the position to do so.
We want to continue to negotiate. We are not going to be able to negotiate from a policy of weakness. If we have a chance for survival at all in this world today it is by maintaining a nuclear deterrent of the utmost possible strength on the part of every country in NATO and to make sure the other side knows what that policy is.

But since 1957 for some and 1958 for others, there have been no increase whatsoever. I do want to point out this entirely abnormal situation to the minister.
Mr. Chairman, I do not know what is going on elsewhere but I have put on the order paper this week questions about the wages paid particularly in North Bay, Ont., St. Hubert, Quebec, Comox, B.C., and at the military colleges of Royal Roads and Kingston. When the minister has given me the information, I will be able to make comparisons, but in any case, one bad situation is no excuse for another.
At the R.C.A.F. base as well as at the military college in my constituency, waitresses, assistant cooks, kitchen labourers, truck drivers and others, are paid absolutely inadequate wages that do not allow them to provide a decent living or even bare necessities for their families.
In the past, that is before 1957, those employees who were not under the civil service had the opportunity to work overtime; they then earned much higher salaries.
In fact, a truck driver told me that in 1955, for instance, he made $1,500 more than he does in 1961.
Furthermore, before 1957, employees who worked on Saturdays and Sundays were getting more, since they were paid time and a half and double time, whereas today they are paid regular salaries as low as 70 cents, 90 cents or a dollar an hour.
Mr. Chairman, I suggest this situation cannot go on any longer especially if we consider that the unemployed get $36 a week from the unemployment insurance fund, while fulltime workers in national defence only get $40 a week. We should reconsider those salaries and give those employees who are devoted servants of the Department of National Defence salaries which should really compare with those of other workers in other fields.
8282	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence
Mr. Chairman, I would also point out that lower salaries are being paid in some areas. For instance, salaries are lower in St. John than in St. Hubert or Quebec City. I wonder why kitchen hands should get less if they work in another area. Yet, the same rate is paid to civil servants, regardless of the area where they work, as well as to servicemen, regardless of the camp where they are posted.
Therefore, I stress that point, and I would like the minister to tell us in his remarks what he intends to do to improve the lot of those honest workers who are forced to work hard without reasonable pay.
Tonight, I wanted to point out that anomaly to the house. I know it is very important during the examination of the estimates of the Department of National Defence to talk about missiles, threats of nuclear warfare and all those troubling things we read about in the newspapers every day, but it is also important, I think, to talk about the fate of those devoted servants of the Department of National Defence. They are often treated as slaves. I am also thinking of the rather sizeable estimates of the Department of National Defence, and of the extravagant expenditures on military hardware and nuclear testing, but I am convinced the government should consider first the situation of the Canadian

citizens who suffer really inferior treatment and I should like the minister to intervene in order to remedy that anomalous situation.
